A1|tenses|Present tense: one form for every person|15,822,840,841,1233,1234,2007,2008,1604,806|Swedish verbs do not change for person: jag bor, du bor, vi bor. Only the verb group matters.|In the present tense the verb has the same form for all persons.¶T:Group¦Ending¦Example//1 (stem in -a)¦-ar¦jag arbet**ar**, du arbet**ar**//2 (consonant stem)¦-er¦jag läs**er**, vi läs**er**//3 (stem in a vowel)¦-r¦jag bo**r**, de bo**r**//4 (strong verbs)¦-er¦jag dricker, hon äter¶**Jag bor i Denver.** (I live in Denver.) **Jag duschar varje morgon.** (I shower every morning.) **Jag läser en bok.** (I am reading a book.)¶• Learn the infinitive and the present together: **att jobba - jobbar**, **att läsa - läser**, **att bo - bor**.¶• Common irregular verbs: **är** (am, is, are), **har**, **kan**, **vill**, **ska**, **går**, **gör**.¶• Tip for English speakers: no -s in the 3rd person! **Hon läser**, not **hon läsers**.
A1|tenses|Present tense means "I do" and "I am doing"|827,840,820,833,834,1622,1629,2035,825,806|Swedish has no continuous form: Jag äter means both I eat and I am eating.|English separates I eat from I am eating. Swedish uses one present tense for both.¶**Jag lyssnar på musik.** (I am listening to music / I listen to music.) **Vi tittar på tv i kväll.** (We are watching TV this evening.) **Jag lagar maten i dag.** (I am cooking today.)¶• For ongoing actions Swedish can add **just nu** (right now) or a verb like **sitta/ligga/stå + och + verb**: **Jag sitter och läser.** (I am sitting reading.)¶• Do not use **är** + verb + -ing like English: not **Jag är äter**.¶• Tip: the context (nu, varje dag, idag) tells you which meaning is meant.
A1|tenses|Present tense for the future|35,476,885,2070,827,1630,2419,4045,2812|Swedish often uses the present tense for future plans, together with a time word.|You can speak about the future with the present tense when there is a time word like **i morgon** (tomorrow) or **på lördag**.¶**Vi ses i morgon!** (See you tomorrow!) **Kommer ni förbi i morgon?** (Are you coming by tomorrow?) **Jag åker till Berlin.** (I am going to Berlin.)¶• For plans you can also use **ska** + infinitive: **Vi ska ut och vandra i helgen.** (We are going hiking at the weekend.)¶• **Kommer att** + infinitive is used for predictions: **Det kommer att regna.** (It is going to rain.)¶• Tip: unlike English will, you do not need an extra word when the time is clear.
A1|tenses|Perfect tense: har + supine|869,870,876,879,881,883,1254,2412,2426,2484,2063,1659|The perfect is har + the supine form: Jag har bokat ett rum. It says what has happened.|Make the perfect with the present of **ha** and the supine of the main verb.¶T:Verb group¦Infinitive¦Supine//1¦boka¦har bok**at**//2¦köpa¦har köp**t**//3¦bo¦har bo**tt**//4 (strong)¦gå¦har gå**tt**, har ä**tit**¶**Jag har bokat ett rum.** (I have booked a room.) **Jag har gått vilse.** (I have got lost.) **Paketet har kommit.** (The package has arrived.)¶• The supine does not change for person: **jag har, vi har, de har gått**.¶• Do not confuse the supine with the past tense: **har gått** (has gone) vs **gick** (went).¶• Tip for English speakers: Swedish uses the perfect for recent events and results, like English. **Har du ätit än?** (Have you eaten yet?)
A1|tenses|Perfect tense for situations that continue|53,54,456,1668,2069,2479,1656,879|Use har + supine, with i + a time, for something that began in the past and still goes on.|English says I have lived here for two years. Swedish does the same, and the situation is still true now.¶**Jag har jobbat här i tre år.** (I have worked here for three years.) **Jag har lärt mig tyska i ett år.** (I have been learning German for a year.) **Vi har varit tillsammans i fem år.** (We have been together for five years.)¶• Use **i** + length of time (**i tre år**, **i tio år**) for how long; use **sedan** + starting point (**sedan 2020**) for since when.¶• Do not use the present tense: **Jag jobbar här i tre år** is wrong in this meaning.¶• Question: **Hur länge har du lärt dig tyska?** (How long have you been learning German?)
A1|tenses|Past tense of vara and ha: var and hade|1259,2480,2486,2490,65,514,4108,130,1287|The past of vara is var; the past of ha is hade. They do not change for person.|These two verbs are the most important ones in the past.¶T:Infinitive¦Present¦Past¦Supine//vara¦är¦var¦varit//ha¦har¦hade¦haft¶**Det var jättegott.** (It was really tasty.) **Vi var i Spanien i två veckor.** (We were in Spain for two weeks.) **Vi hade jättebra samtal.** (We had really good conversations.)¶• One form for every person: **jag var, du var, vi var**; **jag hade, de hade**.¶• Note that the word **var** is also a question word (where). The meaning is clear from the sentence: **Var var du?** (Where were you?)¶• **Hade** is used to build the pluperfect: **Jag hade ätit** (I had eaten).
A1|tenses|Past tense of regular and common irregular verbs|880,2060,2065,2491,4066,4067,457,1826,1824,2507|Regular verbs add -ade, -de or -te; irregular verbs change their vowel.|The past tense (preteritum) is the same for all persons.¶T:Group¦Infinitive¦Past//1¦ringa¦ring**de**; jobba - jobb**ade**//2¦köpa¦köp**te**; höra - hör**de**//3¦bo¦bod**de**//4 (strong)¦gå¦gick; åka - åkte; se - såg¶**Min väckarklocka ringde inte.** (My alarm clock did not ring.) **Jag sprang tio kilometer igår.** (I ran ten kilometers yesterday.) **Förr bodde jag i Wien.** (I used to live in Vienna.)¶• Common irregular verbs: **gå - gick, ta - tog, se - såg, få - fick, göra - gjorde, springa - sprang**.¶• Learn the infinitive, past and supine of each strong verb together.¶• Tip: use the past for finished events with a time word like **igår, förra året**.
A1|tenses|Time words that show the tense|2065,457,35,4066,4067,464,482,822,1681,2079|Words like igår, nu, förra veckan and i morgon help you choose past, present or future.|Swedish verbs do not tell you who does the action, so time words are important.¶T:Time¦Words¦Tense//past¦igår, förra året, häromdagen, förr¦past or perfect//now¦nu, just nu, idag¦present//future¦i morgon, nästa vecka, på lördag¦present or ska//habit¦varje dag, ofta, ibland¦present¶**Jag sprang tio kilometer igår.** (I ran ten kilometers yesterday.) **Han är inte här just nu.** (He is not here right now.) **Vi ses i morgon!** (See you tomorrow!)¶• With **igår** or **förra året** use the past tense; the perfect is not used with a finished time.¶• **Varje, ofta, ibland** tell you about habits: **Jag duschar varje morgon.**
A1|order|Verb second (V2) in statements|15,1604,1607,2419,1234,840,841,822,1622,827|In a main clause the verb is always the second element: Jag bor i Denver.|The most important Swedish word order rule: the finite verb is in second position.¶T:1st¦2nd (verb)¦rest//Jag¦bor¦i Denver.//Vi¦tittar¦på tv i kväll.//Jag¦åker¦buss till jobbet.¶**Jag jobbar på en bank.** (I work at a bank.) **Jag äter frukost klockan åtta.** (I eat breakfast at eight.) **Jag lyssnar på musik.** (I listen to music.)¶• The first position can be one word or a whole phrase (**Min syster** är yngre.). The verb comes next.¶• If you add time or place, the verb still stays second (see the inversion rule).¶• Common mistake: **Jag på en bank jobbar**, which is a word order from German subordinate clauses. In Swedish main clauses it is **Jag jobbar på en bank.**
A1|order|Inversion: verb before subject after a time word|4007,806,4040,4070,4085,4069,4066,4067|If something other than the subject comes first, the verb stays second and the subject follows it.|English says Today I have no time. Swedish says **Idag har jag inte tid** (Today have I no time): the verb comes before the subject.¶T:1st¦verb¦subject//Idag¦har¦jag inte tid.//Nu¦går¦jag och lägger mig.//På vintern¦är¦det kallt.¶**Först äter jag frukost, sedan duschar jag.** (First I eat breakfast, then I shower.) **Förr bodde jag i Wien.** (I used to live in Vienna.) **Efter det går jag till jobbet.** (After that I go to work.)¶• This is called inversion. It happens after time, place and other opening phrases: **Häromdagen såg jag honom.**¶• Do not say **Idag jag har tid**. The verb must come second.¶• Tip: you can always start with the subject or move a time word to the front for variety.
A1|order|Yes/no questions: verb first|18,405,409,830,2008,2407,2442,4006,2805,2830|To ask a yes/no question, put the verb first, before the subject.|English uses do or does. Swedish simply moves the verb to the first place.¶T:Statement¦Question//Du pratar engelska.¦Pratar du engelska?//Det är långt.¦Är det långt?//Du har syskon.¦Har du syskon?¶**Spelar du tennis?** (Do you play tennis?) **Finns det ett hotell här?** (Is there a hotel here?) **Har ni mjölk?** (Do you have milk?)¶• No helping verb do is needed: **Pratar du engelska?**, not **Gör du prata engelska?**.¶• Answers can be short: **Ja, det gör jag**, **Nej, det gör jag inte**, or just **Ja, gärna.**¶• Tip: the intonation goes up at the end of a question.
A1|order|Question words: vad, var, vem, när, hur|10,12,14,16,1611,438,2410,2435,1626,4012,2811,3644|After a question word the verb comes second, directly followed by the subject.|With vad, var, när, hur and other question words the order is: question word + verb + subject.¶T:Question word¦verb¦subject//Vad¦heter¦du?//Var¦bor¦du?//När¦öppnar¦museet?//Hur¦gammal är¦du?¶**När kommer bussen?** (When is the bus coming?) **Var jobbar du?** (Where do you work?) **När ses vi?** (When shall we meet?)¶• Do not add do: **Var du bor?** or **Var gör du bo?** are wrong.¶• **Varför** (why) follows the same rule: **Varför är du ledsen?**¶• When the question word is the subject, there is no inversion: **Vem är det?** and **Vem vann?**
A1|order|Where adverbs go: inte, alltid, bara, också|1220,2006,2821,2036,4007,1218,468,482,3813,3697,3006|In a main clause, short adverbs come right after the verb; in subordinate clauses they come before the verb.|Small adverbs like **inte, alltid, aldrig, bara, också, gärna, ibland** have a fixed place.¶T:Clause¦Order//Main clause¦verb + adverb: Jag gillar **inte** fisk.//Question¦verb + subject + adverb: Gillar du **inte** fisk?//Subordinate clause¦adverb + verb: ...att han **inte** kommer.¶**Jag simmar gärna.** (I like swimming.) **Jag tittar bara.** (I am just looking.) **Jag tränar inte alls.** (I do not exercise at all.) **Idag har jag inte tid.** (Today I have no time.)¶• In subordinate clauses inte comes before the verb: **Jag tycker det är synd att du inte kommer.** (I think it is a pity that you are not coming.) **Det stör mig att han alltid kommer för sent.**¶• Tip: **gärna** is used with verbs to say you like doing something: **Jag dansar gärna.**
A1|order|Starting with the object for emphasis|2822,2823,3667,3668,3820,1257,2880|You can put the object first for emphasis; the verb still stays second.|Normally the subject comes first. To stress an object, move it to the front. The verb must stay in second place, so the subject follows it.¶T:Normal¦Emphasised//Jag gillar den.¦**Den** gillar jag.//Jag tycker det är jättebra.¦**Det** tycker jag är jättebra!¶**Den gillar jag.** (I like that one.) **Den gillar jag inte.** (I do not like that one.) **Det tycker jag inte är bra.** (I do not think that is good.)¶• Used when you contrast, react or refer back to something already said.¶• The first element is often **det** or **den**: **Det vet jag inte**, **Det förstår jag.**¶• Tip: this is very common in spoken Swedish.
A1|verbs|Infinitive with att: gillar att, försöker att|11,1219,2001,52,448,1617,61,848,2030,2086|After many verbs and adjectives, the infinitive is used with att (to).|The infinitive is the basic form of the verb: **spela, äta, träffa**. With **att** in front it means to.¶**Jag gillar att spela fotboll.** (I like to play football.) **Trevligt att träffas.** (Nice to meet you.) **Jag har mycket att göra.** (I have a lot to do.)¶• After verbs like **gilla, älska, börja, sluta, försöka, glömma, hoppas** you use **att**: **Jag älskar att resa.**¶• After adjectives and nouns too: **Det är kul att simma.** **Har du lust att komma förbi?** (Do you feel like dropping by?)¶• **För att** means in order to: **Vädret är perfekt för att springa.** (The weather is perfect for running.)¶• Tip: after modal verbs (kan, vill, ska) there is no att (see below).
A1|verbs|Reflexive verbs with mig, dig, sig|806,811,870,881,3250,3277,457,2063,1671,1685,5965|Some verbs need a reflexive pronoun: mig, dig, sig, oss, er.|The action goes back to the subject.¶T:Person¦Pronoun¦Example//jag¦mig¦Jag lägger mig.//du¦dig¦Sätt dig!//han, hon, den, de¦**sig**¦Hon klär sig.//vi¦oss¦Vi gifte oss.//ni¦er¦Ni ska skynda er.¶**Nu går jag och lägger mig.** (Now I am going to bed.) **Jag känner mig redan bättre.** (I already feel better.) **Jag har skadat mig.** (I have hurt myself.)¶• Only 3rd person uses its own reflexive: **sig**. The others use the normal object pronoun.¶• Common reflexive verbs: **lägga sig, sätta sig, känna sig, skynda sig, försova sig, gifta sig**.¶• Tip for English speakers: Swedish uses more reflexive verbs than English.
A1|verbs|Bli: to become, to get, to turn out|1619,1235,2819,875,3647,3649,3686,4071,1664|Bli means to become, to get or to turn out; it also asks about the total or result.|**Bli** (blir, blev, blivit) is used for changes and results.¶**Jag blir sen.** (I will be late.) **Jag blev så rädd.** (I got so scared.) **Till slut blev allt bra.** (In the end everything turned out fine.)¶• Change of state: **Jag blir glad** (I am becoming happy), **bli klar** (get done).¶• In shops and restaurants **bli** asks about the total: **Hur mycket blir det?** (How much will that be?) **Vad blir det till lunch?** (What will we have for lunch?)¶• **Bli** also builds the passive (see later levels) and means to stay in **bli kvar**.¶• Tip: **bli** is dynamic, **vara** is a state. **Jag är sen** (I am late) vs **Jag blir sen** (I will become late).
A1|verbs|Det finns, det står, det ligger: there is, there are|830,2442,2813,2840,2027,2464|Det finns means there is/there are; ligger, står and sitter say how something is placed.|Swedish has no there is. It uses **det finns** (it exists) or a verb of position.¶**Finns det hiss?** (Is there a lift?) **Finns det ett hotell här?** (Is there a hotel here?) **Var finns det en bankomat?** (Where is there an ATM?)¶• **Det finns** works for singular and plural: **Det finns ett hotell. Det finns tre hotell.**¶• To say where something is, Swedish often uses **ligger** (lies), **står** (stands) or **sitter** (sits): **Det ligger precis runt hörnet.** **Det står två ett.**¶• Tip: **Hotellet ligger i centrum** is more natural than Hotellet är i centrum.
A1|verbs|Verbs with fixed prepositions|827,840,2411,2801,858,1686,1219,1601,3647,3649|Many verbs always take a certain preposition: titta på, lyssna på, leta efter.|Prepositions after verbs are not predictable, so learn the pair.¶T:Swedish¦English//titta på¦look at, watch//lyssna på¦listen to//leta efter¦look for//tycka om¦like//jobba med¦work with, do for a living//vara glad över¦be happy about//vara irriterad på¦be annoyed at¶**Jag lyssnar på musik.** (I listen to music.) **Jag letar efter tunnelbanan.** (I am looking for the subway.) **Vi tittar på tv i kväll.** (We are watching TV tonight.)¶• Common mistake from English: **Jag lyssnar musik** (no preposition) or **Jag letar för...** (wrong preposition).¶• Tip: keep a list and always write the preposition with the verb.
A1|verbs|Present of vara and ha: är and har|17,403,404,407,408,423,426,427,443,444,410,435|Är and har are used for all persons: jag är, du är, vi är; jag har, du har.|**Vara** (to be) and **ha** (to have) are the most important verbs.¶T:Person¦vara¦ha//jag¦är¦har//du¦är¦har//han / hon / det¦är¦har//vi / ni / de¦är¦har¶**Jag är gift.** (I am married.) **Jag har två bröder.** (I have two brothers.) **Vi är en stor familj.** (We are a big family.)¶• Use **är** for identity, job, nationality and state: **Han är min granne.**, **Jag är trettio år gammal.**¶• Use **har** for possession and family: **Vi har en hund.**, **Har du barn?**¶• Ages use **vara**, not ha: **Jag är trettio** (not **Jag har trettio år**).¶• For hunger and cold Swedish uses **vara**: **Jag är hungrig. Jag fryser.**
A1|modal|Kan: can, be able to|85,2427,2438,3237,473,847,855,55|Kan means can or know how to: Kan du hjälpa mig?|**Kan** expresses ability and possibility, and it is also used to ask for help.¶**Kan du hjälpa mig?** (Can you help me?) **Var kan jag växla pengar?** (Where can I change money?) **Jag kan inte sova.** (I cannot sleep.)¶• It has the same form for all persons: **jag kan, du kan, de kan**. The past is **kunde**, the supine **kunnat**.¶• **Kan** is also used for languages and skills: **Jag kan tyska.** (I know German.) The infinitive is not needed there.¶• For permission or polite questions you can use **får**: **Får jag fråga dig en sak?** (May I ask you something?)
A1|modal|Vill and skulle vilja: want, would like|441,1205,2841,1201,1231,1241,2814,1252,2449|Vill is want; skulle vilja is a polite would like.|Use **vill** for a wish, and **skulle vilja** for a polite request.¶T:Form¦Meaning//Jag vill ha kaffe.¦I want coffee.//Jag skulle vilja ha kaffe.¦I would like coffee.//Vill du äta med oss?¦Do you want to eat with us?¶**Vad vill du dricka?** (What do you want to drink?) **Jag vill köpa den.** (I want to buy it.) **Jag skulle vilja betala.** (I would like to pay.)¶• In shops and restaurants **skulle vilja** is more polite: **Vi skulle vilja beställa.**¶• **Vill ha** = want (to have), **vill** + infinitive = want to do.¶• Tip: **Vill du?** can also be an invitation, like English Would you like to?
A1|modal|Måste: have to, must|846,850,1271,1664,2447,3252,3259,3271,4054|Måste means have to; it is also used for strong necessity.|**Måste** expresses an obligation. It is the same for all persons.¶**Jag måste tvätta också.** (I have to wash too.) **Jag måste åka till sjukhuset.** (I have to go to the hospital.) **Måste jag byta tåg?** (Do I have to change trains?)¶• Past: **måste** (same form) or **var tvungen att**. Supine: **måst**.¶• Negation: **inte behöva** = do not have to, **inte få** = must not: **Du behöver inte komma** (You do not have to come) vs **Du får inte komma** (You may not come).¶• Common mistake: **Du måste inte** can mean you must not or do not have to. Use **behöver inte** to be clear.
A1|modal|Ska: plans, intentions and shall we|2812,1276,1654,2044,2070,4045,2448,3256,3270|Ska talks about plans and arrangements, and Ska vi...? makes a suggestion.|**Ska** is used for planned actions, promises and also as a polite question.¶**Jag ska handla.** (I am going shopping.) **Vi ska ut och vandra i helgen.** (We are going hiking at the weekend.) **Vad ska du göra i helgen?** (What are you doing at the weekend?)¶• **Ska vi...?** is a suggestion: **Ska vi gå ut och äta?** (Shall we go out to eat?)¶• **Ska** also asks for instructions: **Hur ofta ska jag ta tabletterna?** (How often should I take the tablets?)¶• It is also used to report what someone tells you to do: **Läkaren säger att jag ska vila.**¶• The past is **skulle**.
A1|modal|Modal verbs take the infinitive without att|85,441,2812,846,3237,2841,1276,3259,2447|After kan, vill, måste, ska, får and other modals the infinitive follows directly, without att.|The modal verbs are followed by the bare infinitive. English also drops to after can, must, but not after want.¶T:Modal¦Example//kan¦Kan du hjälpa mig?//vill¦Jag vill köpa den.//måste¦Jag måste tvätta också.//ska¦Jag ska handla.//får¦Får jag fråga dig en sak?¶**Vill du äta med oss?** (Do you want to eat with us?) **Jag kan inte sova.** (I cannot sleep.) **Jag måste till tandläkaren.** (I have to go to the dentist.)¶• Common mistake: **Jag vill att köpa**. After vill there is no att: **Jag vill köpa**.¶• With other verbs att is needed: **Jag försöker att** (optional), **Jag älskar att resa**.¶• The verb of motion can be left out: **Jag måste till tandläkaren** (= måste gå).
A1|modal|Polite requests with kan, skulle kunna and skulle vilja|85,1201,49,1231,1241,2449,2454,55,1252,2814|Kan du...? is neutral, Skulle du kunna...? is more polite, and Jag skulle vilja... is polite for wishes.|Swedish has several levels of politeness in requests.¶T:Form¦Use//Kan du hjälpa mig?¦neutral, everyday//Skulle du kunna prata långsammare?¦polite//Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe.¦polite wish//Får jag fråga dig en sak?¦polite permission¶**Skulle du kunna prata lite långsammare?** (Could you speak a bit more slowly?) **Jag skulle vilja ha en kaffe, tack.** (I would like a coffee, please.) **Jag skulle vilja checka in.** (I would like to check in.)¶• Add **tack** or **snälla** to be even more polite: **Kan du hjälpa mig, tack?**¶• In shops people often just say the item plus **tack**: **Notan, tack.**¶• Tip: skulle is the past of ska and gives a softer, more distant tone.
A1|articles|Two genders: en and ett|404,435,802,1207,1222,803,1206,1232,1624,2412|Swedish nouns are either en-words or ett-words; the article before a noun means a or an.|Every Swedish noun has a gender, and the indefinite article (a/an) depends on it. There are only two genders.¶T:Gender¦Article¦Example//common (about 75% of nouns)¦en¦en bok (a book), en hund (a dog)//neuter¦ett¦ett hus (a house), ett bord (a table)¶**Vi har en hund.** (We have a dog.) **Vi bor i ett hus.** (We live in a house.)¶• There is no feminine gender: a woman, a girl and a table are all en-words (**en kvinna, en flicka, en säng**).¶• Gender is mostly not logical, so learn each noun with its article: **en kaffe, en öl, ett glas, ett bord**.¶• Rough tip: most nouns are en-words, so **en** is the better guess when you are unsure.¶• Tip for English speakers: gender also decides the definite ending (see the next rule) and how adjectives agree.
A1|articles|The definite form: -en, -n, -et|812,814,821,835,837,1236,2410,1607,2401,845|To say the, Swedish adds an ending to the noun instead of putting a word in front.|English puts the before a noun. Swedish attaches the ending to the end of the noun.¶T:Type¦Indefinite¦Definite//en-word, consonant¦en buss¦buss**en**//en-word, ends in -a¦en flicka¦flicka**n**//ett-word, consonant¦ett brev¦brev**et**//ett-word, ends in vowel¦ett äpple¦äpple**t**¶**Köket är väldigt litet.** (The kitchen is very small.) **Jag åker buss till jobbet.** (I take the bus to work.)¶• If the noun already ends in a vowel, you only add **-n** or **-t**.¶• Many nouns lose an unstressed -e-: **en nyckel - nyckeln**, **en vinter - vintern**.¶• Common mistake: using a separate word like English the (not **den bussen**). With an adjective you use both: **den stora bussen**.
A1|articles|No article: jobs, languages and mass nouns|1609,1603,1602,1636,1243,20,19,18,1233,1217|Swedish leaves out the article for jobs, languages and general uncountable things.|Where English uses a or an, Swedish often uses nothing at all.¶• Jobs and roles: **Jag är ingenjör.** (I am an engineer.) **Jag är student.** (I am a student.)¶• Languages: **Jag pratar lite tyska.** (I speak a little German.)¶• Uncountable things and general likes: **Jag dricker te.** (I drink tea.) **Jag gillar ost.** (I like cheese.)¶• Tip for English speakers: do not add en/ett after **vara** when you name a job: not **Jag är en lärare**, but **Jag är lärare**. With an adjective the article comes back: **Hon är en bra lärare.**¶• After **som** (as) there is no article either: **Jag jobbar som lärare.**
A1|articles|Portions and containers: ett glas vatten|1238,1239,1240,2814,1201,1206,1207,1222,2808|Swedish says a cup coffee: no word for of between the container and what it holds.|English uses of for amounts and containers. Swedish simply puts the two nouns next to each other.¶T:Swedish¦English//en kopp kaffe¦a cup of coffee//ett glas vatten¦a glass of water//en flaska vin¦a bottle of wine//ett kilo äpplen¦a kilo of apples//en bit kaka¦a piece of cake¶**Ett glas rödvin, tack.** (A glass of red wine, please.) **En flaska vatten, tack.** (A bottle of water, please.)¶• The container takes en or ett; the content comes directly after it with no article: **två koppar kaffe** (two cups of coffee).¶• Do not translate of with **av**: **en kopp av kaffe** is wrong.¶• Tip: to order, the item plus **tack** is enough: **En öl, tack.**
A1|nouns|Plural nouns: five endings|815,1615,442,3219,2018,2814,828,410,413|Swedish plurals end in -or, -ar, -er, -n or have no ending; the noun group tells you which.|Swedish nouns fall into five groups. The singular form usually hints at the plural.¶T:Group¦Singular¦Plural//1: nouns in -a¦en flicka¦flick**or**//2: most other en-words¦en bil¦bil**ar**//3: consonant, loanwords, people¦en vän¦vän**ner**//4: ett-words in a vowel¦ett äpple¦äpple**n**//5: most ett-words¦ett hus¦hus (no change)¶**Jag har många vänner.** (I have many friends.) **Lägenheten har tre rum.** (The apartment has three rooms.)¶• Nouns in -e usually take -ar: **en pojke - pojkar**. Nouns in -el/-er often lose the e: **en nyckel - nycklar**.¶• Most ett-words end in a consonant and do not change: **ett barn - två barn**.¶• Learn the plural when you learn the word: **en sak - saker**, **en gång - gånger**.
A1|nouns|Irregular plurals: barn, böcker, föräldrar|403,405,409,413,445,823,5741,5867|Some very common nouns change their vowel or have special plural forms.|A handful of everyday words do not follow the normal endings.¶T:Singular¦Plural//en bok¦böcker (books)//en man¦män (men)//en bror¦bröder (brothers)//en tand¦tänder (teeth)//en förälder¦föräldrar (parents)//ett barn¦barn (children)//ett syskon¦syskon (siblings)¶**Jag har två bröder.** (I have two brothers.) **Mina föräldrar bor i Berlin.** (My parents live in Berlin.)¶• Some words change their vowel in the plural (an umlaut): **en tå - tår, en fot - fötter, en stad - städer**.¶• The ett-words **barn** and **syskon** do not change in the plural, and the definite plural is **barnen**, **syskonen**.¶• Tip: check the dictionary for the plural of every new noun, since the vowel change cannot be predicted.
A1|nouns|Definite plural: -na, -en, -a|2842,445,823,474,865,847,855,2883,3256|To say the + plural, add -na, -en or -a to the plural form.|The definite plural is built on the plural noun. Look at the last letters of the plural.¶T:Plural¦Definite plural//flickor¦flickor**na**//bilar¦bilar**na**//vänner¦vänner**na**//hus¦hus**en**//barn¦barn**en**//äpplen¦äpplen**a**¶**Skorna är fina.** (The shoes are nice.) **Var är barnen?** (Where are the kids?)¶• Plural ending in **-or, -ar, -er** gets **-na**: **flickorna, bilarna, grannarna**.¶• Plural with no ending (ett-words) gets **-en**: **husen, rummen, barnen**.¶• Plural ending in **-n** gets **-a**: **äpplena**.¶• Some irregular words: **tänderna** (the teeth), **männen** (the men).
A1|nouns|Countable and uncountable: många vs mycket|442,446,1617,469,1256,19,859,1656,3223,3232|Use många with plural nouns you can count and mycket with things you cannot count.|Swedish keeps countable and uncountable things apart, just like English many and much.¶T:Type¦Word¦Example//countable (plural)¦många, några, få¦många vänner (many friends)//uncountable¦mycket, lite¦mycket tid (a lot of time)¶**Jag har många vänner.** (I have many friends.) **Jag har mycket att göra.** (I have a lot to do.)¶• **Lite** (a little) goes with uncountables: **lite bröd**. **Få** (few) goes with plurals: **få människor**.¶• **Mycket** is also an adverb: **Jag sover mycket.** (I sleep a lot.)¶• Common mistake: **mycket vänner**. Friends can be counted, so use **många**.
A1|nouns|Compound nouns and their gender|801,814,826,2401,2409,2417,2032,1627,1628,1637|Swedish glues words together into one long noun; the last part decides the gender.|Swedish writes compound words as one word. The last part is the main word and gives the gender and the plural.¶T:Parts¦Compound¦Gender//bad + rum (ett)¦badrummet¦ett//tåg + station (en)¦tågstation¦en//flyg + plats (en)¦flygplats¦en//sjuk + hus (ett)¦sjukhus¦ett¶**Var ligger tågstationen?** (Where is the train station?) **Var är badrummet?** (Where is the bathroom?)¶• Never write the parts apart like English: **tågstation**, not **tåg station**. This is the most common spelling mistake in Swedish.¶• Sometimes a linking letter is added: **dagstidning**, **flickvän**.¶• Tip: look at the last element to find the gender, then add the ending: **tågstationen**, **sjukhuset**.
A1|pronouns|Subject pronouns: jag, du, han, hon, vi, ni, de|9,12,427,443,444,1246,476,2830,2805|Swedish has seven personal pronouns for the subject, plus den, det and man.|The subject pronoun stands in front of the verb and tells you who does the action.¶T:Person¦Singular¦Plural//1st¦jag (I)¦vi (we)//2nd¦du (you)¦ni (you)//3rd¦han, hon, den, det¦de (they)¶**Jag heter Anna.** (My name is Anna.) **Har ni mjölk?** (Do you have milk?) **Hon är min kollega.** (She is my colleague.)¶• **Du** is used for one person, also in polite situations. **Ni** is the plural you and is used for several people or for a shop or restaurant staff.¶• **Man** (one, you in general) is common: **Man ska alltid säga tack.**¶• **De** (they) is usually pronounced dom. Note that **jag** is written with a small letter in the middle of a sentence.
A1|pronouns|Object pronouns: mig, dig, honom, henne, oss, er, dem|85,419,420,441,451,472,473,489,486,55|After a verb or preposition Swedish uses a different form: mig, dig, honom, henne, oss, er, dem.|When a pronoun is the object (not the subject), it changes form.¶T:Subject¦Object//jag¦mig (me)//du¦dig (you)//han / hon¦honom / henne (him / her)//vi¦oss (us)//ni / de¦er / dem (you / them)¶**Jag älskar dig.** (I love you.) **Kan du hjälpa mig?** (Can you help me?) **Vill du äta med oss?** (Do you want to eat with us?)¶• The same forms are used after prepositions: **med mig**, **till dig**, **av henne**.¶• Common mistake in spoken Swedish: mixing up **dig** and **er** with plural you. **Ni** is subject, **er** is object.¶• These forms are also the reflexive forms for 1st and 2nd person: **Jag lägger mig.**, **Sätt dig!**
A1|pronouns|Possessives: min, mitt, mina|43,401,412,413,436,411,813,815,1627,1635,466|Possessives agree with the noun: min (en), mitt (ett), mina (plural).|Possessives come before the noun and match its gender and number.¶T:Owner¦en-word¦ett-word¦plural//my¦min bil¦mitt hus¦mina böcker//your¦din bil¦ditt hus¦dina böcker//our¦vår bil¦vårt hus¦våra böcker¶**Det här är min mamma.** (This is my mother.) **Mitt rum ligger på övervåningen.** (My room is upstairs.) **Var är mina nycklar?** (Where are my keys?)¶• **Hans, hennes, deras** (his, her, their) never change: **hans bil, hennes hus**.¶• The noun after a possessive stays indefinite: **min syster**, not **min systern**.¶• For something belonging to the subject of the sentence, 3rd person uses **sin, sitt, sina**: **Han älskar sin pappa.** (his own father).
A1|pronouns|The pronouns den and det|2802,2804,2822,2823,818,819,2803,4009,40,1229|Den replaces en-words, det replaces ett-words; det also starts impersonal sentences.|Swedish has no it. Instead you use den (for en-words) or det (for ett-words).¶• **Jag köper en jacka. Den är för dyr.** (I am buying a jacket. It is too expensive.)¶• **Jag har ett hus. Det är stort.** (I have a house. It is big.)¶• **Det** is used for impersonal statements: **Det är kallt.** (It is cold.) **Idag är det måndag.** (Today is Monday.) And for identifying: **Det är min mamma.**¶• **Den** and **det** are also objects: **Jag tar den.** (I will take it.) **Den gillar jag inte.** (I do not like it.)¶• Tip for English speakers: do not use den for a thing that is an ett-word: **Huset är stort. Det är gammalt.**
A1|pronouns|This and these: den här, det här, de här|1221,2437,2441,43,401,414,417,1614,46|Den här, det här and de här point at something near you; they agree with the noun.|To say this or these, Swedish uses a demonstrative before the noun, followed by här (here).¶T:Noun¦Singular¦Plural//en-word¦den här gatan¦de här gatorna//ett-word¦det här tåget¦de här tågen¶**Är det här tåget till Köln?** (Is this the train to Cologne?) **Vad heter den här gatan?** (What is this street called?)¶• The noun after the demonstrative is in the definite form (**gatan**, **tåget**).¶• **Det här är** (this is) is used for introductions and stays the same: **Det här är min fru.** (This is my wife.)¶• For something far away use **där**: **den där bilen** (that car).¶• Formal alternatives: **denna, detta, dessa**.
A1|pronouns|Question words: vad, vem, vilken, var, när, hur|10,6,14,843,1205,2011,2424,4008,3644,1626,16,2819|Swedish question words start with v (vad, vem, var, vilken, varför) or h (hur).|Question words come first in the sentence, and the verb follows right after them.¶T:Word¦Meaning¦Example//vad¦what¦Vad heter du?//vem¦who¦Vem är det?//var¦where¦Var bor du?//när¦when¦När är mötet?//hur¦how¦Hur mår du?//varför¦why¦Varför är du ledsen?//vilken / vilket / vilka¦which¦Vilken dag är det?¶• **Vilken** goes with en-words, **vilket** with ett-words and **vilka** with plurals: **Vilken storlek har du?**, **Vilket spår?**.¶• Do not mix up **var** (where) with **vad** (what), and **när** (when) with **om** (if).¶• **Hur** is used in many fixed phrases: **hur gammal, hur mycket, hur länge**.
A1|adjectives|Adjectives after är: kall, kallt, kalla|1229,1236,2842,1615,812,814,835,818,819,2433,1639,3618|After vara, the adjective agrees with the noun: add -t for ett-words and -a for plurals.|When the adjective stands alone after a verb like är, it matches the subject.¶T:Subject¦Form¦Example//en-word¦basic form¦Maten är kall.//ett-word¦+ -t¦Brödet är färskt.//plural¦+ -a¦Skorna är fina.¶**Köket är väldigt litet.** (The kitchen is very small.) **Mina kollegor är trevliga.** (My colleagues are nice.)¶• Adjectives ending in a stressed vowel add -tt: **ny - nytt**; in -d they change to -tt: **god - gott**, **röd - rött**. Adjectives already ending in -t (like **intressant**) usually add nothing: **Det är intressant.**¶• Tip for English speakers: English adjectives never change, so check gender and number every time.
A1|adjectives|Adjectives before a noun: en stor, ett stort, stora|423,802,1624,2835,2031,39,416,858,478,4044|Before a noun, the adjective takes the same -t or -a ending as after är.|In the indefinite form, the adjective agrees with the noun it stands in front of.¶T:Form¦Example//en-word¦en stor familj (a big family)//ett-word¦ett nytt jobb (a new job)//plural¦nya skor (new shoes)¶**Jag bor i en liten lägenhet.** (I live in a small apartment.) **Jag har ett nytt jobb.** (I have a new job.) **Jag köper nya skor.** (I am buying new shoes.)¶• In the definite form the adjective ends in **-a** for all genders and you need a word like den/det/de in front: **den nya skon, det nya jobbet**, **min bästa kompis**.¶• After **mitt, din** etc. the adjective also ends in -a: **min bästa kompis**.¶• Common mistake: **en nytt jobb**. Check if the noun is en or ett.
A1|adjectives|Irregular adjectives: liten, bra, gammal, god|2827,812,1214,1213,1247,4044,1624,7,3613,5194|Some very common adjectives have irregular forms or do not change at all.|A few frequent adjectives are irregular.¶T:en¦ett¦plural//liten¦litet¦små//gammal¦gammalt¦gamla//god¦gott¦goda//ny¦nytt¦nya//bra¦bra¦bra¶**Jag bor i en liten lägenhet.** (I live in a small apartment.) **Det smakar gott.** (It tastes good.) **Gott nytt år!** (Happy new year!)¶• **Bra** (good) and other adjectives ending in a stressed -a do not change: **en bra bok, ett bra jobb, bra skor**.¶• Adjectives ending in -el, -en, -er lose the -e- in the plural and definite: **en gammal - gamla**, **en vacker - vackra**.¶• Tip: learn the three forms together with the adjective.
A1|adjectives|Comparing: äldre, bättre, mer, bäst|424,425,3230,3277,2845,2846,1256,2860,3664|Add -are and -ast to short adjectives, use mer and mest for long ones, and learn bättre/bäst.|Swedish compares adjectives like English.¶T:Basic¦Comparative¦Superlative//gammal¦äldre¦äldst//ung¦yngre¦yngst//bra¦bättre¦bäst//dyr¦dyrare¦dyrast//intressant¦mer intressant¦mest intressant¶**Min bror är äldre än jag.** (My brother is older than me.) **Jag mår bättre.** (I feel better.) **Min syster är yngre.** (My sister is younger.)¶• Use **än** (than) after the comparative: **Boken är bättre än filmen.**¶• Long adjectives (ending in -isk, -ande, -full) use **mer** and **mest** instead of the endings.¶• Common mistake: **mer bra**. Use **bättre**.
A1|adjectives|Intensifiers: väldigt, för, så, lite|812,819,2802,3620,2037,426,3634,1230,468,1247,2826|Words like väldigt, mycket, för and lite make an adjective stronger or weaker.|These small words go before the adjective.¶T:Word¦Meaning¦Example//väldigt, jättebra¦very¦Köket är väldigt litet.//för¦too¦Den är för dyr.//så¦so¦Jag är så glad.//lite¦a bit¦Han är lite blyg.//riktigt¦really¦Det smakar riktigt gott!¶**Det är för varmt.** (It is too hot.) **Jag är väldigt snabb.** (I am very fast.)¶• **För** means too, not for. **Det är för starkt** = it is too strong.¶• **Jätte-** and **super-** can be added directly: **jättetrevlig, jätteorolig**.¶• **Mycket** can mean very or a lot: **Hon är mycket snäll.** (She is very kind.) **Jag sover mycket.** (I sleep a lot.)
A1|preps|Places and directions: i, på, till, från|15,13,1608,1604,2419,2420,803,1637,2444,829,2440|I is inside, på is on or at an open place or event, till is toward and från is from.|The same prepositions often work differently from English, so learn them in fixed phrases.¶T:Word¦Use¦Example//i¦in, inside¦i Denver, i ett hus//på¦on, at (places, institutions)¦på kontoret, på banken//till¦to (direction)¦till Berlin, till jobbet//från¦from¦från USA¶**Jag bor i Denver.** (I live in Denver.) **Jag åker till Berlin.** (I am going to Berlin.) **Jag kommer från USA.** (I come from the USA.)¶• **På** is used for buildings where you do an activity (**på sjukhuset, på kontoret, på banken**), for streets and floors, and for islands.¶• **I** is used for cities, countries and enclosed spaces.¶• Common mistake: **Jag är i kontoret**. Say **Jag är på kontoret.**
A1|preps|Time expressions: i, på, klockan, om|807,1234,4015,4016,4014,4039,4040,4041,439,450,1606,35|Swedish uses klockan for clock times, på for parts of the day and weekdays, i for months and seasons.|Time prepositions are very fixed, so learn them as phrases.¶T:Phrase¦Example//klockan + hour¦klockan sju (at seven)//på + part of the day¦på morgonen, på kvällen//på + weekday¦på lördag (on Saturday)//i + month¦i juni, i maj//på + season¦på sommaren, på vintern//i + tomorrow/weekend¦i morgon, i helgen¶**Jag går upp klockan sju.** (I get up at seven.) **Min födelsedag är i juni.** (My birthday is in June.) **På vintern är det kallt.** (In winter it is cold.)¶• Use **om** for in a future time: **om två dagar** (in two days).¶• Tip: no preposition is needed before **nästa** and **förra**: **nästa vecka, förra veckan**.
A1|preps|med, utan, hos and från|441,431,1223,1224,13,12,2440,2023,1226,1601|Med is with, utan is without, hos is at someone's place and från is from.|These four small words are used all the time.¶T:Word¦Meaning¦Example//med¦with¦Med mjölk, tack.//utan¦without¦Utan socker.//hos¦at someone's home / with a person¦hos mina föräldrar//från¦from¦Jag kommer från Kanada.¶**Vill du äta med oss?** (Do you want to eat with us?) **Vi äter hos mina föräldrar i dag.** (We are eating at my parents' today.)¶• **Hos** is used with people: **hos läkaren** (at the doctor), **hos frisören**. English uses at or to someone's place.¶• **Från** tells where something or someone is from: **Var kommer du ifrån?** Here **från** moves to the end of the question.¶• **Med** and **utan** are also common verb particles: **Följer du med?** (Are you coming along?)
A1|conj|Och and eller: and, or|861,1272,2422,2423,1248,860,806,1276|Och joins things, eller offers a choice; both can join words, phrases and clauses.|**Och** (and) joins two or more things. **Eller** (or) gives a choice.¶**Lägenheten är ljus och lugn.** (The apartment is bright and calm.) **Vi behöver mjölk och ägg.** (We need milk and eggs.) **Enkel eller tur och retur?** (Single or round trip?)¶• **Och** is often pronounced ock. It also joins two verbs: **Nu går jag och lägger mig.** (Now I go and lie down.) **Ska vi gå ut och äta?** (Shall we go out and eat?)¶• When joining two main clauses, word order does not change: **Jag städar och jag diskar.**¶• Commas are not used before och in a list: **äpplen, päron och bananer.**
A1|conj|Men: but|286,5965,6130,6186,6315,653|Men connects two contrasting statements. The word order after men stays normal.|**Men** (but) is a coordinating conjunction: it does not change the word order. The second clause starts with the subject and verb as usual.¶**Jag är ganska stressad, men annars bra.** (I am quite stressed, but otherwise fine.) **Historien upprepar sig inte, men den rimmar.** (History does not repeat itself, but it rhymes.) **Det stämmer förvisso, men det räcker inte.** (That is true, but it is not enough.)¶• A comma is usual before **men** when it joins two main clauses.¶• **Men** can start a sentence: **Men man kan dra lärdom av den.**¶• Do not confuse **men** (but) with **men** (damage, rare) and **man** (one).
A1|conj|Att: that|3613,3614,3636,3663,3671,203,212,3817,5516|Att introduces a subordinate clause after verbs like tycka, tro, hoppas and säga.|**Att** (that) begins a subordinate clause. It can usually not be left out in Swedish.¶**Jag tycker att det är bra.** (I think that it is good.) **Jag hoppas att det går bra.** (I hope it goes well.) **Jag tycker att han är trevlig.** (I think he is nice.)¶• The word order in the subordinate clause is subject + (adverb) + verb: **Jag tror att han inte kommer.** (I think he is not coming.)¶• Unlike English, **att** is also the word for to + infinitive (see the verb rules). Context shows which one it is.¶• Common mistake: leaving att out. **Jag tror han kommer** is informal but possible; in writing use att.
A1|conj|När, om, innan: time and condition|2066,2860,3006,4104,4108,113,2896,2221,108|När is when, om is if, innan is before; they start subordinate clauses.|These small words begin a subordinate clause.¶T:Word¦Meaning¦Example//när¦when¦Jag badar när det är varmt.//om¦if¦Går det bra om det blir lite mer?//innan¦before¦Innan vi går måste jag duscha.//eftersom¦because¦eftersom det regnar¶**Hör av dig när du har tid.** (Get in touch when you have time.) **Kan jag lämna tillbaka den om den inte passar?** (Can I return it if it does not fit?)¶• **När** also means when in questions (**När öppnar museet?**), but **om** also means about/in: **Om en vecka** (in a week).¶• In the subordinate clause, inte and other adverbs come before the verb.¶• If the subordinate clause comes first, the main clause starts with the verb: **När jag var liten hade jag en hund.**
A1|neg|Inte after the verb|21,42,1215,1216,1218,1645,2408,3201,3231,3237,4007|Inte goes after the verb in main clauses: Jag vet inte.|To negate a sentence, put **inte** after the finite verb.¶T:Positive¦Negative//Jag vet.¦Jag vet **inte**.//Jag gillar fisk.¦Jag gillar **inte** fisk.//Det är långt.¦Det är **inte** långt.¶**Jag förstår det inte.** (I do not understand it.) **Jag äter inte kött.** (I do not eat meat.) **Jag kan inte sova.** (I cannot sleep.)¶• When there is a pronoun object, **inte** can come after it: **Jag förstår det inte** (and also **Jag förstår inte det**).¶• Inte never needs do: no **Jag gör inte vet**.¶• In subordinate clauses inte comes before the verb: **att du inte kommer**.
A1|neg|Ingen and inga: no, none, nothing|832,2809,2839,26,1644,2879,3253,57,87,58|Ingen, inget and inga mean no or none; ingenting means nothing.|**Ingen** (en-words), **inget** (ett-words) and **inga** (plural) replace inte + a/any.¶T:Form¦Use¦Example//ingen¦en-word¦ingen balkong//inget¦ett-word¦inget problem//inga¦plural¦inga kontanter//ingenting¦nothing¦Det gör ingenting.¶**Vi har ingen balkong.** (We do not have a balcony.) **Jag behöver ingen påse.** (I do not need a bag.) **Jag har inga kontanter.** (I have no cash.)¶• Do not use a double negative: **Jag har inte ingen** is wrong, say **Jag har ingen**.¶• Typical phrases: **Inga problem. A1|neg|Aldrig and frequency words|822,2002,2041,464,482,468,1690,4073,4027,4029,4028,4030|Alltid, ofta, ibland and aldrig say how often; they stand after the verb in main clauses.|Frequency adverbs tell how often something happens.¶T:Word¦Meaning//alltid¦always//ofta¦often//ibland¦sometimes//sällan¦rarely//aldrig¦never¶**Jag duschar varje morgon.** (I shower every morning.) **Vi ses inte så ofta.** (We do not see each other that often.) **Vi bråkar ibland.** (We argue sometimes.) **Jag spelar varje lördag.** (I play every Saturday.)¶• In main clauses they stand right after the verb: **Han är ibland lite blyg.**¶• **Aldrig** is already negative, so it replaces inte: **Jag äter aldrig kött**, not **Jag äter inte aldrig kött**.¶• Time expressions with varje: **varje dag, varje vecka**.
A1|neg|Short answers: Jag tror det, Jag tror inte det|74,75,29,30,2817,42,31,64|Answer briefly with ja, nej, jo, or Jag tror det / Jag tror inte det.|Swedish short answers are quick and often polite.¶T:Answer¦Meaning//Ja, gärna.¦Yes, please.//Nej tack.¦No thanks.//Jag tror det.¦I think so.//Jag tror inte det.¦I do not think so.//Jag vet inte.¦I do not know.//Kanske.¦Maybe.¶**Ja, gärna.** (Yes, please.) **Nej, det var allt.** (No, that is all.) **Jag tror det.** (I think so.) **Jag tror inte det.** (I do not think so.)¶• Use **jo** to say yes to a negative question: **Gillar du inte fisk? - Jo, det gör jag.**¶• **Det** stands for the whole idea: **Jag tror det**, **Jag hoppas det**.¶• **Tack** means thanks and also please: **Nej tack.**
A1|mood|Imperative: commands and directions|810,811,816,817,2404,2405,2406,76,78,89,477|The imperative is the verb stem: Kom in! Sätt dig! A1|mood|Please: snälla, tack and är du snäll|804,805,852,853,816,22,23,1202,25,1206|Swedish makes requests polite with tack, snälla or är du snäll after the request.|Swedish has no single please. A1|numbers|Numbers 1-20 and the tens|17,418,403,410,828,412,2013,2018,2818,2843,1606|Learn noll to tjugo and the tens; numbers above 20 are built in a regular way.|Swedish numbers are simple to learn.¶T:Number¦Word¦Number¦Word//1¦ett (en)¦11¦elva//2¦två¦12¦tolv//3¦tre¦13¦tretton//4¦fyra¦14¦fjorton//5¦fem¦15¦femton//6¦sex¦16¦sexton//7¦sju¦17¦sjutton//8¦åtta¦18¦arton//9¦nio¦19¦nitton//10¦tio¦20¦tjugo¶**Jag är trettio år gammal.** (I am thirty years old.) **Vi har två barn.** (We have two children.)¶• Tens: **trettio, fyrtio, femtio, sextio, sjuttio, åttio, nittio**. A1|numbers|Telling the time: klockan|4001,4002,4003,4004,4005,842,1640,1641,2425,2015,807|Say Klockan är tre; use halv for half an hour before and kvart for a quarter.|To ask the time, say **Vad är klockan?** To answer, use **Klockan är** and the hour.¶T:Time¦Swedish//3:00¦Klockan är tre.//3:15¦kvart över tre (quarter past three)//3:30¦halv fyra (half to four)//3:45¦kvart i fyra (quarter to four)//3:05¦fem över tre//3:55¦fem i fyra¶**Klockan är halv fyra.** (It is half past three.) **Klockan är kvart i åtta.** (It is quarter to eight.)¶• **Halv** means half to the next hour, not half past: **halv fyra** is 3:30. A1|numbers|Days, months, dates and ordinals|4008,4009,4010,4011,439,4041,4014,438,2041,3612,2872|Days and months are written with a small letter; dates use den första, den andra and so on.|Days and months are not capitalised in Swedish.¶T:Days¦Months//måndag, tisdag, onsdag¦januari, februari, mars//torsdag, fredag¦april, maj, juni//lördag, söndag¦juli, augusti, september, oktober, november, december¶**Idag är det måndag.** (Today is Monday.) **Idag är det den första maj.** (Today is 1 May.) **Jag fyller år i maj.** (My birthday is in May.)¶• Ordinals: **första, andra, tredje, fjärde, femte, sjätte ... tionde, tjugonde**. A1|punct|Capital letters: names yes, days and languages no|9,3,13,15,417,20,18,2440,4009,3612,439|Swedish capitalises names and places, but not days, months, languages or nationalities.|Swedish uses fewer capital letters than English.¶• Capital: names and places: **Anna, Lisa, Denver, Kanada**.¶• Small letter: days and months: **måndag, juni**.¶• Small letter: languages and nationalities: **tyska, engelska, svensk**.¶• Small letter: titles: **fru Müller**, **doktor Berg**.¶**Jag heter Anna.** (My name is Anna.) **Jag pratar lite tyska.** (I speak a little German.) **Idag är det måndag.** (Today is Monday.)¶• Unlike English I, **jag** has a small letter in the middle of a sentence.¶• Common mistake from English: writing **Tyska, Måndag, Juni** with a capital. A1|punct|The letters å, ä and ö, and sj-/tj- sounds|6,807,812,1204,3203,3209,2404,2405,3236,3224,1203|Swedish has three extra vowels at the end of the alphabet, and sj- and tj- are pronounced in special ways.|The Swedish alphabet ends with **å, ä, ö**. A2|tenses|Present tense: one form for all persons|14,15,19,413,431,461,462,465|The present tense has no person endings: jag bor, du bor, vi bor; verbs end in -ar, -er or -r.|Swedish verbs do **not** change with the subject. Mina föräldrar **bor** i Berlin. Hon **pratar** lite tyska. Min son **går** i skolan.¶• Group 1 (-ar): prata – pratar. Group 2 (-er): äta – äter. Group 3 (short verbs): bo – bor. A2|tenses|Past tense (preteritum): -ade, -de, -te|880,1199,457,4067,5701,214,455|Regular verbs form the past with -ade (group 1), -de or -te (group 2); the form is the same for all persons.|The past tense (**preteritum**) describes finished events.¶T:Group¦present¦past//1¦pratar¦pratade//2 (voiced stem)¦bor¦bodde//2 (voiceless stem)¦hör¦hörde//2b¦köper¦köpte//3¦tror¦trodde¶Examples: Min väckarklocka **ringde** inte. (My alarm did not ring.) Förr **bodde** jag i Wien. (I used to live in Vienna.) Vi **gifte** oss förra året. (We got married last year.)¶• Group 1: ending **-ade** (spelade).¶• Group 2: **-de** after a voiced consonant, **-te** after a voiceless one (köpte, åkte).¶• All persons use the same form: jag bodde, vi bodde, de bodde.¶Typical time words: igår, förra året, förr, för två år sedan.
A2|tenses|Irregular past forms: var, hade, tog, fick, vann|65,798,1826,2004,2062,2065,214,3686,4071|Many frequent verbs change their stem vowel in the past: vara – var, ta – tog, få – fick, vinna – vann, springa – sprang.|Group 4 verbs have irregular past forms. (I got such a fright.)¶• Pattern: i – a – u (springa, vinna, sitta) and a – o – a (ta, fara).¶• English speakers: this group is also irregular in English, but the forms are different.
A2|tenses|Perfect tense: har + supine|876,879,881,1656,2063,2479,456,878,869,854,870|The perfect is har + the supine of the verb: jag har köpt, jag har sovit, jag har varit.|The perfect (**perfekt**) is built with **har** (never är) and the **supine**, which is the verb's third form.¶T:Group¦infinitive¦perfect//1¦prata¦har prata**t**//2¦höra¦har hör**t**//3¦bo¦har bo**tt**//4¦sova¦har sov**it**¶Examples: Jag **har köpt** frallor. (I have bought bread rolls.) Jag **har sovit** dåligt. (I slept badly.) Jag **har varit** i Paris förut. (I have been to Paris before.) Jag **har skadat** mig. (I have hurt myself.)¶• The supine does not change with the subject or number: jag har köpt, vi har köpt.¶• **Har** is the only helper for all verbs in standard Swedish, even for movement: Jag har åkt till Paris. (Not är.)¶• Supine endings: -at (group 1), -t (group 2), -tt (group 3), -it (many group 4).
A2|tenses|Perfect for duration: har ... i / sedan|53,54,1668,2069,3248,3400,491,456|Use the perfect with i + a period or sedan + a starting point to say how long something has lasted.|When something started in the past and is **still true now**, Swedish uses the present perfect (not the present tense as in some languages).¶• **i + period**: Jag **har lärt** mig tyska **i** ett år. (I have been learning German for a year.) Jag har jobbat här **i** tre år.¶• **sedan + starting point**: Jag har haft ont i halsen **sedan** i går. (I have had a sore throat since yesterday.) Vi har känt varandra **sedan** skoltiden.¶• **Hur länge har du ...?** (How long have you ...?): Hur länge har du haft feber?¶• Vi har varit tillsammans i fem år. (We have been together for five years.)¶Mistake: Jag lär mig tyska i ett år. Say **Jag har lärt mig** tyska i ett år.
A2|tenses|Preterite or perfect? Finished vs linked to now|457,2065,4067,455,2479,456,876,1668|Use the past for a finished time; use the perfect when the result or period still matters now.|Both tenses translate to English past or perfect, so think about the time.¶T:Preterite (finished)¦Perfect (linked to now)//Vi gifte oss förra året.¦Vi har varit tillsammans i fem år.//Jag sprang igår.¦Jag har köpt frallor.//Förr bodde jag i Wien.¦Jag har varit i Paris förut.¶• Use **preteritum** with a definite past time: igår, förra året, 1989.¶• Use **perfekt** with no time, or with 'before now', or for a period up to now: Jag har varit i Paris förut. Jag har jobbat här i tre år.¶• A time word like **just now** needs the perfect: Jag har precis vaknat.¶Tip: Swedish uses the perfect more often than English, e.g. for results: Jag har köpt frallor (so we have them).
A2|tenses|Talking about plans: ska + infinitive|2070,4045,1654,121,106,2448,3270,1276|Ska + infinitive expresses plans and intentions: Vi ska ut och vandra i helgen.|**Ska** (from skola) is the standard way to speak about what you plan to do.¶• **Plans**: Vi **ska** ut och vandra i helgen. A2|tenses|Future: present tense and kommer att|35,476,885,2078,2883,4006,6029,6031|Swedish often uses the present for the future with a time word; kommer att adds a prediction.|Swedish has no true future tense. Vi **har** match imorgon.¶• **Kommer att + infinitive** for predictions and facts about the future: Man **kommer att** se tillbaka på den här tiden. (People will look back on this time.) A2|order|Verb second (V2) in main clauses|15,462,413,876,2419,1602,2070,455|In a main clause the finite verb is always the second element, whatever comes first.|The **finite verb** (the one that shows tense) sits in second position in every main clause.¶T:1st¦2nd (verb)¦rest//Jag¦bor¦i Denver.//Min son¦går¦i skolan.//Vi¦träffades¦på universitetet.//Jag¦har köpt¦frallor.¶• The first slot can hold more than one word: **Mina föräldrar** bor i Berlin.¶• With a helper verb the helper is second and the main verb comes last: Vi **ska** ut och **vandra** i helgen.¶• Questions and statements with a time word obey the same rule (see the next rule).¶Tip: English is SVO; Swedish is V2. When you start with something other than the subject, swap subject and verb: **Idag** är allt nedsatt.¶Mistake: Idag jag bor här. Say **Idag bor jag här.**
A2|order|Inversion: verb before subject after adverbs|2867,806,222,111,4067,3694,1631,2421|If a time or place word starts the clause, the verb comes next and the subject follows it.|When something other than the subject is first, the verb still stays second, and the **subject comes after it** (inversion).¶T:first¦verb¦subject¦rest//Idag¦är¦allt¦nedsatt.//Nu¦går¦jag¦och lägger mig.//Tyvärr¦måste¦jag¦gå nu.//Förr¦bodde¦jag¦i Wien.//Här¦är¦mitt¦cv.¶Examples: **Nu** ska **jag** låta dig jobba vidare. A2|order|Place and time after the verb|457,2065,1668,2479,3400,2070,2483,431|After the verb the order is: subject, verb, (object), then manner, place and time.|In the middle of the clause, expressions are stacked. A2|order|Inte and adverbs before the verb in subordinate clauses|3813,3006,5644,3697,5306,5871,6015,208,229|In a subordinate clause the adverb or inte comes before the finite verb: att du inte kommer.|In main clauses **inte** and other adverbs come **after** the verb: Du kommer **inte**. A2|verbs|Infinitive with att|2001,1728,2030,2086,5560,5510,6226,6335|Att is the infinitive marker (like English to); after modal verbs and gärna it is left out.|The infinitive is the base form of the verb (tala, äta, gå). Jag gillar **att** jobba i team.¶• After adjectives and nouns: Vädret är perfekt **för att** springa. (The weather is perfect for running.) Man är aldrig för gammal **för att** lära sig.¶• Purpose: Jag läser tyska böcker **för att** utöka mitt ordförråd.¶• **No att** after modal verbs (kan, ska, vill, måste, bör, får) and after **låta, se, höra**: Jag kan sova. Jag ser honom komma.¶• Placement: Jag gillar inte att jobba. (**inte** before att).¶Mistake: Jag vill att gå. Say **Jag vill gå.**
A2|verbs|Reflexive verbs in sentences and tenses|806,881,2063,870,89,5191,5192,5306|Reflexive verbs keep their pronoun in every tense; in the perfect it sits after har + supine.|The reflexive pronoun stays with the verb in all tenses.¶T:tense¦example//present¦Jag lägger **mig** nu.//past¦Jag la **mig** sent.//perfect¦Jag har försovit **mig**.//imperative¦Skynda **dig**! (One minute, please.)¶• **Containers and measures**: no word for 'of'. **En flaska vatten** (a bottle of water), **en bit kaka** (a piece of cake), **ett kilo äpplen** (a kilo of apples).¶The agreement follows the measure word, not what is inside: ett kilo, en flaska.¶Tip: another coffee is **en kaffe till**.
A2|nouns|Plurals: -or, -ar and -er|2480,3249,4035,3219,3265,2055,4081,2890,2835|Most nouns add -or, -ar or -er in the plural, depending on their ending and group.|Swedish has five plural groups. The three most common endings are:¶T:Ending¦typical nouns¦example//-or¦en-words ending in -a¦en vecka – veckor, en flicka – flickor, en sko – skor//-ar¦en-words ending in -e, -el, -en, -er, and many others¦en dag – dagar, en timme – timmar//-er¦nouns ending in a consonant, foreign words¦en katt – katter, en biljett – biljetter¶Examples: Vi var i Spanien i två **veckor**. (We were in Spain for two weeks.) Jag är allergisk mot **katter**. (I am allergic to cats.) Jag behöver fem **minuter** till. (I need five more minutes.)¶• Words in -a nearly always form the plural with -or.¶• Words in unstressed -are and -ande are unchanged: en lärare – lärare.¶Tip: learn the plural together with the singular for each new noun.
A2|nouns|Plurals: -n and no ending|410,409,828,1272,456,1668,5573,2814|Ett-words ending in a vowel add -n; most other ett-words stay unchanged in the plural.|Two plural patterns belong to ett-words and a few special nouns.¶• **-n**: ett-words ending in a vowel add -n: ett äpple – äpplen, ett piano – pianon. Example: Jag skulle vilja ha ett kilo **äpplen**. (I would like a kilo of apples.)¶• **No ending**: ett-words ending in a consonant do not change at all: ett barn – två **barn**, ett rum – tre **rum**, ett ägg – fyra **ägg**, ett år – fem **år**.¶Examples: Vi har två **barn**. (We have two children.) Lägenheten har tre **rum**. (The flat has three rooms.)¶You can only see that a word is plural from the number or from the verb and context, so numbers matter: Jag har jobbat här i tre **år**. (I have worked here for three years.)¶• Also unchanged: en lärare – lärare.¶Mistake: tre barns, två rums. Do not add -s.
A2|nouns|Definite plural: -na and -en|445,2842,855,3256,865,823,847,1195,2883,4086|Add -na, -a or -en to the plural to say "the ...s": flickor – flickorna, äpplen – äpplena, barn – barnen.|For the definite plural you add an ending to the indefinite plural form.¶T:Plural ending¦definite plural¦example//-or¦-orna¦blomma – blommorna//-ar¦-arna¦granne – grannarna//-er¦-erna¦nyckel – nycklarna; tablett – tabletterna//-n¦-na¦äpplen – äpplena//no ending (ett-word)¦-en¦barn – barnen, rum – rummen¶Examples: Skor**na** är fina. (The shoes are nice.) Kan du vattna blommor**na**? (Can you water the plants?) Var är barn**en**? (Where are the children?)¶Tip for English speakers: the plural of a definite noun also has no extra article: **tabletterna**, not de tabletterna, unless an adjective is added (de nya skorna).¶Common mistake: leaving out the vowel, as in bilarna – say all of -arna.
A2|nouns|Irregular plurals: man – män, bok – böcker|403,2415,669,2685,5253,5560|A small group of very common nouns changes the vowel in the plural: man – män, bok – böcker, tand – tänder.|A handful of everyday nouns form the plural with a **vowel change** (umlaut), often with -er added.¶T:Singular¦plural//en man¦män//en bror¦bröder//en bok¦böcker//en fot¦fötter//en tand¦tänder//en hand¦händer//en natt¦nätter//en son¦söner¶Examples: Jag har två **bröder**. (I read German books.)¶• Some of these also have a regular form in speech: händer, tänder – these are the standard ones.¶• In the definite plural add the usual ending: böckerna, männen, tänderna.¶Tip: these words are the ones you meet every day, so learn them as pairs. A2|pronouns|Personal pronouns: jag/mig, du/dig, han/honom|419,2427,489,472,473,2870,1289,424,3687,1649,486|Swedish pronouns change form as object: jag becomes mig, du dig, han honom, hon henne, vi oss, de dem.|Most pronouns have a **subject form** (before the verb) and an **object form** (after verbs and prepositions).¶T:Subject¦Object¦Example//jag¦mig¦Kan du hjälpa **mig**?//du¦dig¦Jag älskar **dig**.//han¦honom¦Vad kan jag ge **honom**?//hon¦henne¦Hälsa **henne** så gott.//vi¦oss¦Jag beställer pizza till **oss**.//ni¦er¦Jag hör **er**.//de¦dem¦Jag ser **dem**.//den, det¦den, det¦Jag tar **den**.¶Examples: Jag skickar dokumenten till **dig**. (You scared me!)¶• Use han/hon for people, **den** for things that are en-words and **det** for ett-words.¶• After than and as, colloquial Swedish uses the subject form: äldre än **jag** (older than me).¶Mistake: Kan du hjälpa jag? Use **mig** after a verb.
A2|pronouns|Possessives: min, mitt, mina, din, vår|402,414,436,421,431,813,834,1627,1635,2421,815,1615|Possessives stand before the noun and agree with it: min bil (en), mitt hus (ett), mina nycklar (plural).|A possessive comes **before** the noun and agrees with it in gender and number, not with the owner.¶T:person¦en-word¦ett-word¦plural//my¦min¦mitt¦mina//your¦din¦ditt¦dina//our¦vår¦vårt¦våra//your (pl.)¦er¦ert¦era//his, her, their¦hans, hennes, deras¦hans, hennes, deras¦hans, hennes, deras¶Examples: Det här är **min** pappa. (This is my father.) Jag städar **mitt** rum. (I am tidying my room.) Var är **mina** nycklar? (Where are my keys?)¶• **Hans, hennes and deras never change**: hans bil, hans hus, hans barn.¶• Do not combine the possessive with an article. You say **min bil**, never den min bil. With body parts Swedish often uses the definite form instead: Jag borstar tänderna. (I brush my teeth.)¶Tip: the English habit of 'my' stays: Vår katt heter Mia. (Our cat is called Mia.)
A2|pronouns|Reflexive possessives: sin, sitt, sina|466,794,5738,5427,5911,5948,5177,5281,500|Use sin, sitt or sina when the owner is the subject of the sentence; use hans/hennes/deras for someone else.|When the possessor is the **subject of the same clause** and is third person (han, hon, de, a name), Swedish uses **sin / sitt / sina** (own).¶• Han är lik **sin** pappa. (He looks like his [own] father.)¶• Hon har uppfostrat **sina** barn. (She has raised her [own] children.)¶• De väntar **sitt** andra barn. (They are expecting their second child.)¶Compare: Han träffade **hans** pappa. means he met another man's father. Han träffade **sin** pappa. means his own father.¶T:Owner¦en-word¦ett-word¦plural//subject (3rd person)¦sin¦sitt¦sina//other person¦hans/hennes¦hans/hennes¦hans/hennes/deras¶• Sin agrees with the thing owned, like min: sin bok, sitt hus, sina barn.¶• It does not exist for jag, du, vi: there you use min, din, vår as usual.¶Tip: English has no such distinction, so this can feel unnecessary, but the difference is real.
A2|pronouns|This, that and which: den här, det där, vilken|401,1221,2437,46,4010,2424,1285,2822,2804,2823|Den här / det här / de här mean "this", den där / det där "that", and vilken / vilket / vilka ask "which".|Swedish demonstratives agree with the noun and have two parts.¶T:Meaning¦en-word¦ett-word¦plural//this¦den här¦det här¦de här//that¦den där¦det där¦de där//which¦vilken¦vilket¦vilka¶Examples: Är **den här** platsen ledig? Here det är is a fixed phrase and never changes.¶• **Den / det / de** alone often means 'that' or 'it': Den gillar jag. (I like that one.) Jag tar **den**. (I'll take it.)¶• Vilken and vilket ask about a specific thing: Vilken storlek? (Which size?) Vilket spår? (Which platform?)¶Tip: in writing you also see denna / detta / dessa, but den här and det här are normal in speech.
A2|pronouns|Reflexive verbs with mig, dig, sig|806,457,4058,89,3250,3277,3659,5676,1248|Some verbs need a reflexive pronoun: mig, dig, sig, oss, er, sig; sig is used for han, hon, de, man and den.|The reflexive pronoun repeats the subject.¶T:Subject¦reflexive¦Example//jag¦mig¦Jag lägger **mig**.//du¦dig¦Du skyndar **dig**.//han, hon, den, man¦sig¦Hon känner **sig** trött.//vi¦oss¦Vi gifte **oss**.//ni¦er¦Ni ser **er**.//de¦sig¦De känner **sig** ensamma.¶Examples: Nu går jag och lägger **mig**. A2|adjectives|Adjective agreement before a noun: stor, stort, stora|802,423,5462,1673,4044,2031,2835,2863,5194,5358,5405|An adjective takes -t with ett-words and -a in the plural: en stor bil, ett stort hus, stora bilar.|Adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number.¶T:Noun¦form¦Example//en-word¦stor¦en **stor** familj//ett-word¦stor**t**¦ett **stort** glapp//plural¦stor**a**¦**stora** framsteg¶Examples: Vi har ett **nytt** projekt. A2|adjectives|Adjectives after verbs: Det är kallt, Skorna är fina|818,819,866,2842,3607,2802,812,1639,2043,2826,2827,426|After är, var, blir the adjective still agrees with the subject: Vattnet är kallt, Skorna är fina.|After a linking verb (är, var, blir) the adjective also agrees, but it comes after the noun.¶T:Subject¦Example//en-word¦Den är för dyr.//ett-word¦Vattnet är kall**t**.//plural¦Skorna är fin**a**.//det¦Det är fin**t**.¶Examples: Köket är väldigt **litet**. A2|adjectives|Special -t forms: viktigt, rätt, fel, nöjt|3640,3616,3617,3638,3639,3631,2803|Most adjectives add -t, but some are unchanged (rätt, fel, intressant, stolt) and some change (röd – rött).|The -t ending has a few special cases.¶• **Add -t**: viktig – viktig**t**, tråkig – tråkig**t**, billig – billig**t**.¶• **Unchanged** when the word already ends in -t after a vowel or in -nt: rätt, intressant, stolt, fel, trött. Det är **intressant**. (It is interesting.) Det är **rätt**. (It is correct.)¶• **-d becomes -tt**: röd – rött, god – gott, ledsen – ledset (-en becomes -et).¶• **-a, -s** words do not change: bra, lila, gratis.¶Examples: Det är **viktigt** för mig. (It is important to me.) Jag är **stolt**. (I am proud.) Det är **fel**. (That is wrong.)¶Tip: do not translate the -t rule word for word from English; adjectives ending in -ig are the common group that just takes -t.
A2|adjectives|Adjective + definite noun: den stora bilen|1287,5354,5944,5981,201,4118,5628,5472,6398,2463|With an adjective and a definite noun use den/det/de + adjective in -a + noun with ending: den stora bilen.|Swedish marks 'the' twice in this pattern: a separate article **and** the ending on the noun.¶T:Gender¦indefinite¦definite//en-word¦en stor bil¦den stora bilen//ett-word¦ett stort hus¦det stora huset//plural¦stora hus¦de stora husen¶• The adjective always ends in **-a** in this pattern.¶Examples: Jag är **den nya grannen**. A2|adjectives|Comparison: större, störst, bättre, bäst, mer|424,425,2845,3230,3277,5712,5167,5503,5662,1287,5622,5730|Add -are and -ast to short adjectives; use mer and mest with longer ones; learn bra – bättre – bäst.|Swedish compares like English.¶T:Positive¦Comparative¦Superlative//stor¦större¦störst//snabb¦snabbare¦snabbast//ung¦yngre¦yngst//bra¦bättre¦bäst//mycket¦mer¦mest//liten¦mindre¦minst//gammal¦äldre¦äldst¶• **-are / -ast** for most adjectives: Priserna stiger **snabbare** än lönerna. A2|preps|Place: i and på|15,413,432,1604,2087,1637,1608,2871,2010,462,455,2444|Use i for cities, countries and enclosed spaces; use på for open places, institutions, workplaces and events.|The two most common place prepositions are **i** (in) and **på** (on, at).¶• **i**: cities, countries and things you are inside: Jag bor **i** Denver. Vi spelar **i** parken. Min son går **i** skolan. (My son goes to school.)¶• **på**: workplaces and institutions, open surfaces and events: Jag jobbar **på** en bank. Jag är **på** kontoret. Jag är **på** stranden. Vi träffades **på** universitetet.¶• Many fixed phrases must be learned: **på** sjukhuset, **på** gym, **på** jobbet, **i** skolan, **på** torget.¶Direction does not change the preposition for these places, but the verb does: Jag **är** på kontoret, Jag **går** till torget.¶Tip: English at/in/on does not map one to one, so learn the common place with its preposition together.
A2|preps|Direction and origin: till, från, hos|2420,2403,2437,2067,2460,2419,13,2440,1606,431,463,3269,481|Till means to, från means from, and hos means at someone's place.|Movement towards a place uses **till**, movement away or origin uses **från**.¶• **till**: Jag åker **till** Berlin. (I am going to Berlin.) Jag cyklar **till** jobbet. (I cycle to work.) Hur kommer jag **till** hotellet? (How do I get to the hotel?)¶• **från**: Jag kommer **från** Kanada. (I come from Canada.) Jag jobbar **från** nio **till** fem. (I work from nine to five.)¶• **hos** is used for people and their homes: Vi äter **hos** mina föräldrar. (We eat at my parents' place.) Jag var **hos** läkaren. (I was at the doctor's.)¶• **Hem** (home) uses no preposition for direction: Jag går hem. But you say Jag är hemma (I am at home).¶Mistake: Jag åker i Berlin. Say **till Berlin**.
A2|preps|Time: i, på, om, för ... sedan|439,450,4052,4039,4016,4056,1664,54,456,4062,4063,4085,446|Months and durations take i; days and parts of the day take på; om means "in" for the future; sedan means "ago".|Time prepositions are different from English, so learn them in groups.¶• **i** for months, duration and 'this week': Jag fyller år **i** maj. Vi träffar vänner **i** helgen.¶• **på** for days, seasons and parts of the day: Vi har fest **på** lördag. **På** sommaren reser jag bort. **På** kvällen. **På** eftermiddagen.¶• **om** for something in the future: Jag är där **om** tio minuter. (I'll be there in ten minutes.) **Om** en vecka. (In a week.)¶• **för ... sedan** means 'ago': **För** två år **sedan**. (Two years ago.)¶• **till** gives a deadline: Jag måste bli klar med det här **till** fredag.¶Mistake: Vi ses i måndag. Say **på måndag**.
A2|preps|Other common prepositions: med, utan, för, av, mot, om|1224,1223,440,452,3265,3258,3681,3688,487,3634,3648,3645,1666|Many verbs and adjectives need a fixed preposition; learn them together: tacksam för, rädd för, allergisk mot.|Besides place and time, prepositions often depend on the word before them. A2|conj|Och, men, eller: joining clauses|64,2422,1248,5344,5559,5965,6284|Och, men, eller and för join main clauses without changing the word order.|These conjunctions connect words or clauses and do **not** affect the verb order.¶T:word¦meaning¦example//och¦and¦Jag bor i Berlin och jobbar på en bank.//men¦but¦Jag förstår nästan allt, **men** jag tycker det är svårt att prata.//eller¦or¦Enkel **eller** tur och retur?//utan¦but (after negative)¦Vi lär oss inte för skolan **utan** för livet.//för¦because¦Jag är trött, **för** jag sov dåligt.¶• After the conjunction the order is normal: Pengar gör en inte lycklig, **men de lugnar**.¶• **Utan** replaces men after a negative that contradicts: Hem är ingen plats **utan** en känsla.¶• Use a comma before **men**, and before **och** only when two full clauses have different subjects.¶Tip: repeat the subject, or leave it out when it is the same: Jag äter och dricker.
A2|conj|Att: that-clauses|3270,3681,3813,5516,5511,6042,6044,6051,229|Att introduces a clause that says what someone thinks, says, knows or feels.|**Att** works like English 'that', but you must not leave it out as casually as in English.¶• After verbs of saying and thinking: Läkaren säger **att** jag ska vila. (I'm glad you are here.)¶• After adjectives and nouns: Jag tycker det är synd **att** du inte kommer.¶• Word order in the that-clause: subject first, then adverb/inte, then verb: ...**att** du **inte** kommer.¶• Often **att** can be dropped in speech but not in writing: Jag tror (att) han kommer.¶Mistake: Jag vet att jag vet ingenting. A2|conj|Om, när, medan: if and when|113,208,1006,4103,2221,2896,6342,2860,67|När = when, om = if, medan = while. (I broke my arm when I was skiing.)¶• **Om** is for conditions: Går det bra **om** det blir lite mer? (Is it OK if it's a bit more?)¶• The subordinate clause can come first, and then the main clause has verb-first order: **Om** du har några frågor, **är** du välkommen att kontakta oss.¶Mistake: Om jag kom hem, ringde jag. Use **när** for a real time (when I came home).
A2|conj|Som: relative clauses|5244,5306,5468,6015,1679,86,5514,5243,5871|Som links a noun to extra information: Den som spelar högt kan falla djupt.|**Som** is the all-purpose relative word, for people and things, as subject or object.¶• **Den som** (the one who / whoever): **Den som** spelar högt kan falla djupt. (...that cannot be said in words.)¶T:English¦Swedish//who, which, that¦som//whose¦vars//what¦vad¶Mistake: Den mannen som han ... Do not repeat the pronoun.
A2|conj|Linking words: därför, dessutom, således|6058,6052,6150,6146,6141,6125|Därför, dessutom, således and andra linking adverbs join ideas; the verb comes straight after them.|Linking words (**sambandsord**) are adverbs, so they start the clause and the verb follows at once (V2 + inversion).¶T:word¦meaning¦example//därför¦therefore¦**Därför** föreslår jag att vi väntar.//dessutom¦in addition¦**Dessutom** råder det brist på personal.//således¦thus¦**Således** är beslutet rätt.//icke desto mindre¦nevertheless¦**Icke desto mindre** borde vi försöka.//ändå¦still¦Det gick **ändå** bra.¶• After the linking word comes the verb, then the subject: Därför **föreslår jag** ...¶• In writing, put a comma after longer ones: Dessutom, bör man tänka på ...¶Tip: in speech, people prefer **så**, **också** and **men**. A2|neg|Inte: negating a verb|880,1199,3237,42,1681,464,116,1400|Inte comes after the verb in a main clause: Jag vet inte. Han är inte här.|**Inte** (not) is the normal word for negation.¶• After the finite verb: Jag vet **inte**. (I don't know.) Han är **inte** här just nu. Vi ses **inte** så ofta.¶• After a helper verb it comes before the infinitive: Jag kan **inte** sova. (I can't sleep.) Min väckarklocka ringde **inte**.¶• In the perfect: Jag har **inte** sovit. (I haven't slept.)¶• With a question: Stör jag **inte**? (Am I not disturbing you?)¶• There is no helper **do/don't**: Jag vet inte, not Jag gör inte veta.¶T:statement¦negative//Jag vet.¦Jag vet **inte**.//Han är här.¦Han är **inte** här.//Jag kan sova.¦Jag kan **inte** sova.¶• In subordinate clauses inte moves before the verb (see the earlier rule).¶Tip: for the structure inte + noun use ingen/inget (next rule): Det är **inget** för mig.
A2|neg|Ingen, inget, inga, aldrig: no and never|26,58,87,1644,2809,3253,4028,5516|Ingen/inget/inga mean "no" or "none" before a noun; ingenting is "nothing" and aldrig "never".|Use these words when the thing does not exist.¶T:Word¦meaning¦example//ingen (en-word)¦no / none¦Jag behöver **ingen** påse. A2|punct|Commas, question marks and quotation marks|1,3,29,41,47,50,64,67,1644,4069,1652|Use a comma after greetings and between two full sentences; Swedish uses ordinary quotation marks.|Swedish commas follow fewer fixed rules than in English or German.¶• **After a greeting or yes/no**: Hej, hur är det? B1|tenses|Har varit: being and experience|456,607,625,2212,2479,4114|Har varit covers states that continue until now and life experiences: jag har varit i Paris.|**Har varit** (supine of vara) is used for a state that began in the past and still continues, and for experiences.¶• Vi **har varit** tillsammans i fem år. B1|tenses|Present tense for future events|525,862,885,1018,1672,1691,476,449|Swedish often uses the plain present with a future time word: Vi flyttar nästa månad.|When a future time is clear from the sentence, Swedish uses the **present tense**, just like English "I am leaving tomorrow".¶• Vi **flyttar** nästa månad. B1|tenses|Perfect or simple past?|54,1668,4067,535,2670,2479,2896,2556|Perfect links the past to now (no finished time); preteritum is for finished events with a past time.|The choice looks like English, with a few small differences.¶T:Use¦Tense¦Example//finished event, time given¦preteritum¦Vi träffades förra året.//still true now, or experience¦perfect¦Jag har bott här i tre år.¶• Jag **har** lärt mig tyska i ett år. Common mistake: using the perfect with a question about a finished time: say När kom du?, not "När har du kommit?".
B1|order|Verb second (V2) in main clauses|619,1018,1672,1691,2532,623,2482,1760|In a main clause the finite verb is always in second position.|The golden rule of Swedish word order: in a main clause, the finite (conjugated) verb is the **second element**. The first element can be a subject, an adverb or an object.¶T:1st¦2nd (verb)¦Rest//Jag¦tar¦semester nästa vecka.//Nästa vecka¦tar¦jag semester.//Vi¦ska¦gå ut i kväll.¶• Hyresvärden **kommer** förbi i morgon. (The landlord is coming by tomorrow.)¶• Jag **tar** semester nästa vecka. (I am taking leave next week.)¶• Hotellet **ligger** centralt. (The hotel is centrally located.)¶• Vi **ska** gå ut i kväll. (We are going out tonight.)¶• Jag **ska** sätta igång det. (I will get it started.)¶The "first element" counts as one unit, however long it is. When something other than the subject is first, the subject moves after the verb (see inversion). Common mistake: copying English order, "I tomorrow come" or "Nästa vecka jag tar".
B1|order|Inversion after adverbials|4007,2272,3849,1843,4049,4387,4388,4155,4287|If an adverbial comes first, the verb stays second and the subject follows it: Idag har jag inte tid.|When you start a sentence with something other than the subject (a time word, a place, a clause), the verb still comes second and the subject comes **after** the verb. This is called **inversion**.¶T:1st¦verb¦subject¦rest//Idag¦har¦jag¦inte tid.//Då¦kan¦jag¦tyvärr inte.//Sedan dess¦har¦mycket¦förändrats.¶• **Idag har jag** inte tid. (I do not have time today.)¶• **Idag orkar jag** inte träna. (Today I cannot be bothered to work out.)¶• **Då får du** vända dig till min kollega. (Then you will have to turn to my colleague.)¶• **Då och då unnar jag** mig en ledig dag. (Now and then I treat myself to a day off.)¶• **Sedan dess har mycket** förändrats. (A lot has changed since then.)¶Common mistake: leaving the subject in front, as in English: "Idag jag har inte tid". The same inversion follows an introductory subordinate clause: När jag kom hem, åt jag. (When I got home, I ate.)
B1|order|Adverbs in subordinate clauses|3813,4247,2758,1103,5644,3006,208|In a subordinate clause, inte and other sentence adverbs come BEFORE the finite verb.|This is a key difference between main and subordinate clauses in Swedish.¶T:Clause¦Order//main clause¦subject + verb + inte: Jag kommer inte.//subordinate¦subject + inte + verb: ... att jag inte kommer.¶• Jag tycker det är synd att du **inte kommer**.
