(I am late because the bus did not come.)¶• Jag trampade i klaveret eftersom jag **inte kände** till sederna. (I put my foot in it because I did not know the customs.)¶• Kan jag lämna tillbaka den om den **inte passar**? (Can I return it if it does not fit?)¶• Vad brukar du göra när du **inte jobbar**? (What do you usually do when you are not working?)¶The same applies to **aldrig, alltid, också, ofta, bara, redan**: ... eftersom han alltid kommer sent. Common mistake: copying the main-clause order, "att du kommer inte". Tip: to remember, picture inte as a small word that hurries ahead of the verb after att, om, när, eftersom, som.
B1|order|Question word order|121,421,445,815,1665,2460,2473,2863|Question words go first, then the verb, then the subject: Var är barnen?|In a question that starts with a question word (hur, var, när, vem, vad, varför), the verb follows right after it and then comes the subject.¶T:Question word¦Verb¦Subject¦Rest//Hur¦mår¦din familj¦?//Var¦kan¦jag¦parkera?//Vad¦gör¦du¦i helgen?¶• **Hur mår** din familj? Common mistake: "Var jag kan parkera?" which keeps statement order, or inserting "gör".
B1|order|Yes/no questions: verb first|441,428,1458,476,3402,232,49|Yes/no questions start with the verb: Vill du äta med oss?|A question without a question word starts with the **finite verb**, then the subject. Common mistake: using a rising tone with statement order only, which is a casual option in speech but is wrong in careful writing.
B1|order|Fronted objects|1091,249,360,1854,2822,2880,1257,3668,2509,6363|Put the object first for emphasis; the subject then follows the verb: Det där ger jag bort.|Swedish can move the object to the front of the sentence to stress it or to link back to what was said. B1|verbs|Infinitive with and without att|3428,2091,1079,3316,2638,986,6403,1460|Most verbs take att before an infinitive; modal verbs and a few others take the bare infinitive.|In Swedish the infinitive marker is **att** (like English "to"). (See you, as they say.)¶**No att** after modal verbs (kan, ska, vill, måste, bör, får) and after a few others such as **brukar, behöver (often), börjar, låter**: Jag brukar gå. In speech att is often left out after försöka, börja, sluta, but it is always safe to write it. After **för** use **för att** for purpose: Jag tränar för att må bra. B1|verbs|Bli: becoming and getting|525,648,875,1354,1433,5325,1619,3686,4071,3649|Bli means become, get or turn out; the past is blev and the supine blivit.|**Bli** is one of the most useful Swedish verbs. B1|verbs|Reflexive verbs with sig|616,3857,271,499,20,806,3250,3659,2847|Reflexive verbs need mig, dig, sig, oss, er, sig: jag känner mig, hon lugnar sig.|Many Swedish verbs are reflexive: the object is the same person as the subject. B1|verbs|Få: get, receive, be allowed to|1888,2681,2164,5381,1655,1684,115,55,3297|Få means receive or get, and with an infinitive it means be allowed to or have the chance to.|**Få** (får, fick, fått) has several uses.¶T:Use¦Example//receive, get¦Jag har fått jobbet.//catch, suffer¦Jag fick magsjuka.//be allowed to¦Får jag fråga dig något?//be affected by something¦Han fick sparken.¶• Jag **fick** magsjuka på semestern. (I would like a kilo of apples.)¶Helpful tendencies: nouns ending in **-a** take -or (flicka, flickor); nouns ending in **-are** or **-e** often take -ar or -n; most ett-words ending in a consonant have no plural ending. Tip: some nouns change vowel too (en bok, böcker; en man, män).

B1|nouns|Definite forms: -en, -et, -na, -en|911,1064,2929,445,560,3419,3074,2173,526|The definite ending is attached to the noun: singular -en/-n/-et/-t, plural -na or -en.|In Swedish "the" is usually an ending on the noun. B1|nouns|Genitive -s: showing possession|697,1402,1251,2163,2247,5623|Add -s to the owner, with no apostrophe: mammas ögon, dagens rätt, lagets stjärna.|Swedish shows possession by adding **-s** directly to the owner. (He is the star of the team.)¶• Han är i **sitt livs** form. (He is in the form of his life.)¶The -s goes on the last word of the whole owner phrase: **min bror Pers** bil (my brother Per's car). With a noun already ending in -s, x or z the form stays unchanged: Hans bok (Hans's book). Tip: the owner comes first and the thing owned second, without a word like "of": **husets tak**, not "taket av huset".
B1|nouns|Compound nouns: one word, last part decides|1087,2470,2471,1803,2501,953,1889,1828,3012|Swedish glues words into one noun; the final part gives the gender and the plural.|Swedish joins nouns into one long word. Common mistake: splitting the word ("medlems kort"), which is an error in Swedish and can change the meaning. Tip: the stress falls on the first part.
B1|pronouns|Subject and object pronouns|55,61,85,95,505,614,64,97|Subjects: jag, du, han, hon, vi, ni, de. B1|pronouns|Reflexive possessive: sin, sitt, sina|466,496,503,642,500,798,6008,5738,5318|Use sin/sitt/sina when the owner is the subject (his own); use hans/hennes/deras for someone else.|When the possessor is the **subject of the same clause** and it is third person (han, hon, den, de), Swedish uses **sin, sitt, sina** instead of hans/hennes/deras.¶T:Meaning¦Form¦Example//his own (subject owns)¦sin/sitt/sina¦Han tar hand om sin mamma.//someone else's¦hans/hennes/deras¦Han tar hand om hennes mamma.¶• Han är lik **sin** pappa. B1|pronouns|Man: the general "you/one"|47,48,83,281,283,6065,6403,5835|Man is the everyday way to say one/you/they in general; it takes the verb in the normal form.|**Man** is a pronoun for people in general. B1|pronouns|Relative clauses with som|955,154,86,493,6257,5794,5691,4665|Som is the all-purpose relative pronoun: who, which and that. It is needed even as subject.|**Som** begins a relative clause. B1|conj|Att-clauses: that|3714,3813,3814,6044,6078,1103,3613,3614,3636|Att introduces a content clause: Jag tror att det går bra. B1|punct|Commas: men, utan and main clauses|159,6315,6130,2565,6097,5965,5344,6134,6186|Put a comma before men and utan, and before a new main clause with its own subject and verb.|Swedish commas follow clause structure more than breathing.¶• A comma before **men** (but) and **utan** (but rather): Det stämmer förvisso**,** men det räcker inte. (That is true, but it is not enough.)¶• Frågan är inte om**,** utan hur. (The question is not whether but how.)¶• Historien upprepar sig inte**,** men den rimmar. (History does not repeat itself, but it rhymes.)¶• Ta inte illa upp**,** men jag måste ställa in. (Don't take offence, but I have to cancel.)¶• Tåget är försenat igen**,** som vanligt. (The train is late again, as usual.)¶There is **no** comma before **att** (that) clauses in standard writing, nor before a relative clause which is essential: Jag känner en man som bor här. A comma goes around non-essential information. Between two main clauses joined by **och** or **eller** the comma is optional: use it when the clauses are long or have different subjects. Common mistake: copying the English comma before "that" or after introductory words like "Nu".
B1|style|Written correspondence phrases|1711,1845,6107,6319,6335,1973,452,6338,1969|Standard phrases for emails and letters: Tack för ..., Bifogat finner du ..., Hör gärna av dig om ...|Swedish formal and semi-formal writing uses well-worn phrases.¶T:Purpose¦Phrase//thanks¦Tack för ditt snabba svar.//attachment¦Bifogat finner du offerten.//reference¦Angående din fråga...//apology¦Vi ber om ursäkt för besväret.//closing¦Hör gärna av dig om du har några frågor.¶• Tack så mycket för ditt snabba svar. (Thank you very much for your quick reply.)¶• **Bifogat finner du** offerten. (Enclosed you will find the quote.)¶• **Angående** din fråga kan jag säga följande. (Regarding your question, I can say the following.)¶• **Vi ber om ursäkt för** besväret. (We apologise for the inconvenience.)¶• **Hör gärna av dig om** du har några frågor. (Please get in touch if you have any questions.)¶Start with **Hej** (casual or neutral) or **Bäste/Bästa** (more formal); Swedish uses du everywhere, even in formal emails. End with **Med vänliga hälsningar** (kind regards) or just **Hälsningar**. Common mistake: using "Kära" (dear) too often; Hej Anna is the normal start.
B1|style|Softening requests and criticism|1698,2505,1970,314,317,1347,1291,2506|Soften with skulle, gärna, tyvärr, kanske and polite openers like Om du tillåter...|Swedish speakers often avoid direct demands. (If you permit, I would like to add something.)¶• Jag **vill inte vara indiskret, men** hur gammal är du? B1|style|Giving opinions: tro, tycka, mena|203,1695,92,3813,3814,3952,3613,3667|Tycker = think/feel (opinion), tror = believe/guess, menar = mean/claim.|Three verbs for "think" with different shades.¶T:Verb¦Meaning¦Example//tycka (tycker)¦opinion, taste¦Jag tycker att det är bra.//tro (tror)¦belief, guess¦Jag tror att vi har träffats förut.//mena (menar)¦mean, claim¦Vad menar du med det?¶• Jag **tror** att vi har träffats förut. B2|tenses|Past perfect: hade + supine|4105,5690,5921,5953,3961,3715,3981,360,249|Use hade + supine for something that happened before another point in the past.|The past perfect (pluskvamperfekt) places one event **before** another past event. It is built with **hade** + the **supine** (the form used after har).¶T:Verb¦Supine¦Past perfect//äta¦ätit¦hade ätit//glömma¦glömt¦hade glömt//tro¦trott¦hade trott//klara¦klarat¦hade klarat¶**När jag hade ätit gick jag ut på en promenad.** (When I had eaten I went for a walk.)¶**Jag hade aldrig trott att det skulle hända.** (I would never have thought it would happen.)¶**Åh, det hade jag nästan glömt!** (Oh, I had almost forgotten that!)¶• The main event is usually in the simple past (gick), the earlier one in the past perfect (hade ätit).¶• Swedish needs hade even in subordinate clauses: ...eftersom han hade lämnat. Unlike spoken English, you cannot just use the simple past.¶• Mistake: using the past participle form: hade ätet. Use the **supine**: hade ätit.¶• The supine ends in -t (-it, -at, -tt) and is the same word you use after har.
B2|tenses|Present perfect for what is still true: har ... sedan, i|456,491,607,2212,3400,3848,701,762,1919|Swedish uses har + supine with sedan (since) and i (for) for situations that began in the past and continue now.|English says I have known him for years. B2|tenses|Perfect (har gjort) or past tense (gjorde)?|2221,3016,2896,1724,878,2488,1344,1823|Use the simple past for a finished time in the past; use har + supine for a result that matters now or for recent news.|Swedish divides the two tenses like English, with one big difference: Swedish speakers use the perfect more freely for recent events and results.¶T:Use¦Tense¦Example//finished time given¦past¦Jag bröt armen när jag åkte skidor.//result now¦perfect¦Jag har brutit armen.//just happened¦perfect¦Vi har precis kommit fram.//story, narrative¦past¦Den var redan trasig när jag köpte den.¶**Jag har blivit befordrad.** (I've been promoted.)¶**Jag har precis vaknat.** (I've just woken up.)¶**Jag har sökt jobb på tre företag.** (I've applied to three companies.)¶• If you name a **finished time** (i går, förra veckan, när jag var liten) use the simple past.¶• **Precis, redan, nyss, hittills** go well with the perfect.¶• Mistake: Jag har gått dit igår. B2|tenses|Talking about the future: ska, kommer att, present tense|619,450,2767,3186,4578,4855,6029,6031,569|Swedish has no future tense: use ska for plans, kommer att for predictions, or the present tense with a time word.|Swedish forms the future with helper verbs or just the present.¶T:Form¦Use¦Example//ska + infinitive¦plan, intention¦Min son ska snart flytta hemifrån.//kommer att + inf.¦prediction, certainty¦Det kommer att kosta mig en förmögenhet.//present + time word¦fixed event¦Vi har fest på lördag.¶**Min son ska snart flytta hemifrån.** (My son is going to move out soon.)¶**Nästa generation kommer att döma oss efter det.** (The next generation will judge us for it.)¶**Jag kommer aldrig att glömma dig.** (I'll never forget you.)¶• **Kommer att** is the neutral will. Jag vill komma = I want to come.¶• In everyday talk the present tense is enough: Jag ringer i morgon.
B2|tenses|Ongoing action: håller på att and pseudo-coordination|2282,3053,733,1872,3385,976,806,2002,2171|Håller på att + infinitive means is in the middle of or about to; sitter/står/går och + verb expresses an ongoing activity.|Swedish has no -ing form, so it uses other patterns.¶**1. B2|order|V2 after a fronted element (inversion)|111,168,169,182,222,235,248,144|The finite verb is always the second element in a main clause, so after an adverb or clause at the start the subject follows the verb.|**Verb second (V2)** is the central rule of Swedish word order: the finite verb takes position 2 in a main clause.¶T:1¦2 (verb)¦3//Jag¦måste¦gå nu.//Tyvärr¦måste¦jag gå nu.//Nu¦ska¦jag låta dig jobba vidare.¶**Tyvärr måste jag gå nu.** (Unfortunately I have to leave now.)¶**Som tur var gick det ändå.** (Luckily it worked out anyway.)¶**Då har vi nog missförstått varandra.** (Then we have probably misunderstood each other.)¶**Såvitt jag vet har han redan gått.** (As far as I know he has already left.)¶• Position 1 can be an adverb, a time phrase, an object, or a whole subordinate clause. B2|order|Adverb position in subordinate clauses: inte before the verb|136,208,236,1103,2758,3006,3813,4256,5644|In subordinate clauses sentence adverbs (inte, aldrig, redan, alltid) come before the finite verb.|This is the big word-order difference between main clauses and subordinate clauses in Swedish.¶T:Main clause¦Subordinate clause//Jag kommer inte.¦...att jag inte kommer.//Hon har redan gått.¦...eftersom hon redan har gått.//Vi åker aldrig.¦...när vi aldrig åker.¶**Jag tycker det är synd att du inte kommer.** (I think it's a pity that you're not coming.)¶**Jag trampade i klaveret eftersom jag inte kände till sederna.** (I put my foot in it because I didn't know the customs.)¶**Jag kan knappt tro att det redan är december.** (I can hardly believe it's December already.)¶• Order in the subordinate clause: **subject + adverb + verb**: att du inte kommer.¶• This also applies to the perfect: ...eftersom hon inte har kommit (inte before har).¶• Mistake: att du kommer inte. B2|order|Fronting the object for emphasis|195,249,360,3981,3103,1854,599,3556|Putting the object first makes it the topic; the verb stays second and the subject follows it.|Swedish often starts a sentence with the **object**, not the subject, to stress it or link to what was just said.¶T:Normal¦Fronted object//Jag hade nästan glömt det.¦Det hade jag nästan glömt!//Jag har inte läst villkoren.¦Villkoren har jag förstås inte läst.//Vi borde skjuta upp det.¦Det borde vi skjuta upp.¶**Det hade jag aldrig trott om dig.** (I would never have thought that of you.)¶**Villkoren har jag förstås inte läst.** (I haven't read the terms, of course.)¶**Homeopati tycker jag är nonsens.** (Homeopathy I find nonsense.)¶• The fronted object is usually a pronoun like **det** or a known noun.¶• V2 still applies: Det (1) hade (2) jag (3) glömt.¶• Don't use this for new information: it works best when the thing was just mentioned.¶• English speakers often forget the inversion and write Det jag hade glömt, which is a relative clause and not a full sentence.

B2|adjectives|Participles as adjectives: -ande and -ad/-at|956,993,1916,1912,1532,1893,1705,1832,967,1015,1920,3046,2138,363|Present participles end in -ande/-ende (spännande); past participles agree like adjectives: -ad, -at, -ade.|Many Swedish adjectives are really verb participles.¶T:Verb¦Present participle¦Past participle//irritera¦irriterande¦irriterad//spänna¦spännande¦spänd//överbelasta¦överbelastande¦överbelastad//begränsa¦begränsande¦begränsad¶**Mögelet i badrummet är irriterande.** (The mould in the bathroom is annoying.)¶**Matchen kunde knappast ha varit mer spännande.** (The match could hardly have been more exciting.)¶**Jag är överbelastad.** (I'm overloaded.)¶**Mitt kontrakt är tidsbegränsat.** (My contract is fixed-term.)¶• **-ande/-ende** is active and never changes: en spännande match, ett imponerande jobb, spännande matcher.¶• **Past participles** agree: -ad (en), -at (ett), -ade (plural/definite): en överbelastad, ett tidsbegränsat avtal, tidsbegränsade avtal.¶• -ande describes what something does (irriterande = it irritates); -ad describes the person affected (irriterad = annoyed).¶• Tip: -ande resembles English -ing, -ad resembles -ed.

B2|conj|När, medan and då: time clauses|2221,2896,3016,2748,1006,4103,113,1080,3479,4350|När means when/whenever, medan means while, and tenses stay in the same time frame as in the main clause.|**När** (when) and **medan** (while) start subordinate clauses, so the word order is subject + adverb + verb.¶T:Conjunction¦Meaning¦Example//när¦when, whenever¦Hör av dig när du har tid.//medan¦while¦Kan du vattna blommorna medan jag är borta?//innan¦before¦Släck lampan innan du går.//efter att¦after¦Efter att jag kom hem åt jag.¶**Jag bröt armen när jag åkte skidor.** (I broke my arm when I was skiing.)¶**Medan du lagar mat dukar jag bordet.** (While you cook, I'll set the table.)¶**Jag får ofta huvudvärk när jag är stressad.** (I often get a headache when I'm stressed.)¶**Det hade redan börjat skymma när vi kom fram.** (It had already got dark when we arrived.)¶• **När** is used for both single events and repeated events; for the second the main clause often has ofta or alltid.¶• Present tense in the clause is used for the future: Hör av dig när du har tid. (not kommer att ha).¶• The tense of the när-clause matches the time you mean: past with past, present with present.¶• **Då** as a conjunction is old-fashioned or literary; use när.

B2|conj|Paired conjunctions: både ... och, varken ... eller, ju ... desto|4679,5747,5990,6111,6112,6113,1377,5515,6114,1396,3987|Both ... and, neither ... nor and the more ... the more are built with fixed pairs.|Pairs link two parts of equal rank.¶T:Pair¦Meaning//både ... och¦both ... and//varken ... eller¦neither ... nor//inte bara ... utan även¦not only ... but also//ju ... desto/ju¦the more ... the more¶**Tekniken är både en välsignelse och en förbannelse.** (Technology is both a blessing and a curse.)¶**Varken den ena eller den andra lösningen är perfekt.** (Neither solution is perfect.)¶**Inte bara kostnaderna utan även arbetsinsatsen är enorm.** (Not only the costs but also the effort is enormous.)¶**Ju längre vi väntar, desto dyrare blir det.** (The longer we wait, the more expensive it gets.)¶• **Ju ... desto** uses comparatives: ju mer, desto mer. B2|conj|Att-clauses after adjectives and verbs: glad att, anser att|3681,3700,3808,3882,3270,3813,3814,3730,6083|Att introduces a that-clause after verbs of saying/thinking and feeling adjectives; in speech the att is often dropped.|Swedish uses **att** where English uses that.¶T:After¦Example//glad¦Jag är glad att du är här.//synd¦Jag tycker det är synd att du inte kommer.//säga¦Läkaren säger att jag ska vila.//anse¦Jag anser att vi borde vänta.¶**Jag är glad att allt gick bra.** (I'm glad everything went well.)¶**Jag är glad att det är över.** (I'm glad it's over.)¶**Man kan mycket väl hävda att det är vettigt.** (One can very well argue that it makes sense.)¶• No preposition is needed after glad: **glad att**, not glad för att (that is only used for reason).¶• Word order in the att-clause: **att + subject + adverb + verb**: att du inte kommer.¶• Att can be left out in speech after verbs like tycka, tro, säga, but not after prepositions or in formal writing: Jag tror (att) han kommer.¶• Mistake: Jag är glad att kommer du. B2|particles|Ju: shared knowledge and emphasis|354,384,395,1599,2057,3759,3890,3983|Ju marks something as obvious or known to both speakers, and adds an emotional tone; it sits after the verb.|**Ju** has no direct English word. It means as you know, after all or of course, and it adds feeling.¶**Domaren är ju blind!** (The referee is blind, for heaven's sake!)¶**Det är ju strunt!** (That's just nonsense!)¶**Man tappar ju andan.** (It really takes your breath away.)¶**Dig känner man ju knappt igen!** (You're hardly recognisable!)¶• Position: ju stands in the middle field, after the finite verb (and before inte in a negative: Det är ju inte sant).¶• Meaning depends on tone: friendly (Du vet ju hur det är), annoyed (Det är ju strunt) or ironic (Det var ju toppen!).¶• Don't confuse with the conjunction **ju ... desto** (the more ... the more).¶• In a subordinate clause ju also goes before the verb: ...eftersom det ju är sant.¶• Overusing ju can sound pushy; use it where the information is really shared.
B2|particles|Nog, väl and visst: guessing and softening|116,235,323,3960,3152,6265,6129,312,6083|Nog (probably), väl (I suppose, surely) and visst (certainly) shade a statement with doubt or expectation.|These small words show how sure the speaker is.¶T:Particle¦Meaning¦Example//nog¦probably, I think¦Mina förväntningar var nog för höga.//väl¦I suppose, surely¦Jag stör väl inte?//visst¦certainly (before a but)¦Visst finns det nackdelar, men fördelarna överväger.//mycket väl¦very well, certainly¦Man kan mycket väl hävda det.¶**Jag uttryckte mig nog otydligt.** (I probably expressed myself unclearly.)¶**Det går nog att göra något åt.** (It's probably possible to do something about it.)¶**Jag är nog mer realist.** (I'm probably more of a realist.)¶• **Nog** softens a claim: Det går nog bra. (It'll probably be fine.)¶• **Väl** often asks for confirmation: Du kommer väl? (You are coming, aren't you?)¶• **Visst** at the start of a sentence concedes a point and expects a but.¶• Don't confuse nog (probably) with the adjective nog (enough): Jag har fått nog.
B2|particles|Egentligen, faktiskt and förresten: fillers with meaning|120,128,204,279,4953,3997,3103|Egentligen (really, actually), faktiskt (in fact) and förresten (by the way) add attitude to a sentence.|These words are everywhere in spoken Swedish.¶T:Word¦Meaning¦Example//egentligen¦actually, really¦Hur känner du Lisa egentligen?//faktiskt¦in fact¦Tiden läker faktiskt många sår.//förresten¦by the way¦Förresten, jag har nyheter.//verkligen¦really¦Behöver jag det verkligen?//förstås¦of course¦Villkoren har jag förstås inte läst.¶**Jag menade egentligen något annat.** (I actually meant something else.)¶**Skämt åsido: Hur mår du egentligen?** (Joking aside, how are you really?)¶• **Egentligen** can express a contrast between what is thought and what is true: Jag menade egentligen något annat.¶• **Faktiskt** stresses that something is true, often surprising: Det är faktiskt sant.¶• **Förresten** starts a new topic in passing.¶• Position: in the middle field, after the verb in main clauses: Jag har faktiskt inte tid.
B2|punct|Commas: before men, utan and fast|159,286,653,5559,5965,6097,6129,2694,537,6024|Swedish uses fewer commas than English: put one before men, utan and fast; none before och.|Swedish comma rules are lighter than English.¶**Comma before main-clause conjunctions of contrast:**¶**Ta inte illa upp, men jag måste ställa in.** (Don't take offence, but I have to cancel.)¶**Historien upprepar sig inte, men den rimmar.** (History doesn't repeat itself, but it rhymes.)¶**Jag längtar redan ut igen, fast jag precis har kommit hem.** (I'm longing to go out again even though I just got home.)¶**Frågan är inte om, utan hur.** (The question is not whether, but how.)¶• **No comma** before och or eller when joining two main clauses with the same subject: Jag lagar mat och han diskar.¶• A comma separates a **subordinate clause that comes first**: När jag kom hem, åt jag. (Often optional.)¶• Use commas in lists, but not before the last item: äpplen, päron och bananer.¶• Mistake: copying the English comma before that or and. Swedish does not use one before that-clauses.

C1|tenses|Pluperfect: hade + supine|4105,4325,790,5690,5921,5953,2748,360,3961,249,3981|Hade + supine places an event before another past point; it also builds unreal conditions and regrets.|The pluperfect is **hade + supine** (the form that ends in -t, -it or -at): **hade ätit**, **hade klarat**, **hade vetat**. C1|tenses|Future with kommer att|2767,3186,3954,4578,4855,4856,6029,6031,6355,6391|Kommer att states a prediction or neutral fact about the future; ska and vill carry plans and will.|Swedish has no single future tense. C1|tenses|Present perfect with sedan and duration|54,456,491,607,701,762,1312,1668,1919,2069,3400|Swedish uses har + supine with i or sedan for situations that began in the past and still hold.|For something that started in the past and **continues now**, Swedish uses the present perfect (**har + supine**), not the simple present as in some languages. C1|order|Fronting the object: Det visste jag inte|73,195,249,360,683,739,1257,1854,3981|Placing the object first for emphasis keeps the verb second and puts the subject after it.|Swedish is a **V2 language**: the finite verb is always the second element in a main clause. C1|order|Subordinate clause first, then verb-subject|136,142,177,4105,4108,1343,337,6121,6122|When a clause opens the sentence, the main clause that follows starts with its verb.|A whole subordinate clause counts as the **first element** of the sentence. C1|articles|Double definiteness with adjectives|201,739,1060,1097,1157,1160,1287,1406,1555,1594|With an adjective, Swedish uses BOTH a preposed den/det/de and the suffixed article: den stora bilen.|In Swedish a definite noun normally ends in the article (**bilen**, **huset**). (The best food.)¶• Possessives and demonstratives replace the free article but keep the noun ending in some cases: **min gamla bil** (no ending), **det här gamla huset**.¶• Mistake for English speakers: saying den stor bil or den stora bil. You need the ending on the noun too: **den stora bilen**.¶• Names and titles can behave differently: **Gamla stan** (the Old Town) has no free article.
C1|articles|Bare nouns: no article after prepositions|513,875,1235,1662,1717,2418,2481,2728,3469,1411|Many fixed expressions drop the article: på semester, på lunch, med tåg, på sjukhus, till middag.|Swedish leaves out the article in many fixed phrases where English would use one, especially after prepositions, when the noun names an activity or a state rather than a particular thing.¶• **på semester** (on holiday): **Jag är på semester.** (I'm on holiday.)¶• **på lunch / till middag** (at lunch / for dinner): **Vad blir det till middag?** (What's for dinner?)¶• **med tåg / med buss / med flyg** (by train, bus, plane): **Med tåg är resan i sig målet.** (By train, the journey is the goal itself.)¶• **på sjukhus** (in hospital): **Jag ligger på sjukhus.** (I'm in hospital.)¶Compare a particular place, where the article returns: **Jag är på kontoret.** (I'm at the office.) **Hur går det på jobbet?** (How is it going at work?) Tip: learn these as chunks, because the rule is not fully predictable. If you add the article to a bare phrase, it changes the meaning: på sjukhuset means at a specific hospital.
C1|articles|No article for professions, but en/ett in judgments|433,1243,4406,4580,4854,5096,1538,3563|After är/blir, jobs and nationalities take no article; abstract judgments take en/ett: en viktig fråga.|English says She is a doctor. Swedish normally drops the article when you state someone's **profession, role, religion or nationality**:¶• **Min faster är läkare.** (My aunt is a doctor.)¶• **Jag är vegetarian.** (I'm a vegetarian.)¶• Also: **Hon blev lärare.** (She became a teacher.)¶But as soon as you add an adjective, or you describe a thing or an idea rather than classify a person, the article comes back:¶• **Barnomsorgen är en viktig fråga.** (Childcare is an important issue.)¶• **Klimaträttvisa är en moralisk fråga.** (Climate justice is a moral question.)¶• **Festmåltiden blev en fullträff.** (The festive meal was a complete success.)¶• **Hon är en bra läkare.** (She is a good doctor.)¶Mistake to avoid: Jag är en lärare. It sounds odd unless you add more information. Remember the two genders: **en** fråga, **ett** problem.
C1|nouns|Unchanged plurals and irregular plurals|403,2685,669,697,3982,4408,5253,5953,5573,500|Many ett-words ending in a consonant do not change in the plural, and some common nouns change vowel.|Swedish has five plural groups. Most nouns add **-or, -ar, -er, -r or -n**, but you must learn which. Two points deserve special attention at C1.¶**1. Unchanged plurals.** Most ett-words that end in a consonant, and many en-words in -are, -er, -el or -en, look the same in singular and plural:¶• **ett barn, två barn** (one child, two children)¶• **ett språk, flera språk** (one language, several languages)¶• **en lärare, två lärare** (one teacher, two teachers)¶**2. Vowel change** (a handful of very common nouns): **en man, män**; **en fot, fötter**; **en tand, tänder**; **en bror, bröder**; **en mor, mödrar**; **ett öga, ögon**.¶**Barn från utsatta familjer är missgynnade.** (Children from disadvantaged families are at a disadvantage.) **Hon har sin mammas ögon.** (She has her mother's eyes.)¶Tip: the definite plural shows the pattern: **barnen, ögonen, männen, fötterna**. Learn the plural together with the noun.
C1|nouns|The genitive -s and the of-construction|697,771,1251,1402,1481,1977,3563,4437,4689,5976|The genitive is formed with -s on the owner; there is no apostrophe, and the owner comes first.|Swedish has no case system, but a noun can take **-s** to show possession. It is attached to the whole noun phrase and has **no apostrophe**: **mammas ögon** (mum's eyes), **chefens högra hand** (the boss's right hand), **dagens rätt** (today's dish).¶• Owner first, then the thing owned: **Mannens förkylning** (the man's cold). **Barnens skärmtid** (the children's screen time).¶• Words already ending in -s, -x or -z stay unchanged: Names ending in -s are unchanged: **Hans bil** (Hans's car), **Max bil**.¶• The alternative is **av** or **till**: **vägen till stationen** (the way to the station), **ägaren till huset**. Use it for things, long phrases and formal style: **ledaren för partiet**.¶• Compare the pronoun: **hans, hennes, deras** are possessives and never take an extra s.¶**Vägen till mannens hjärta går genom magen.** (The way to a man's heart is through his stomach.) Mistake: using an apostrophe like English (mamma's).
C1|pronouns|Generic man|47,184,281,283,354,393,683,759,1120,1175|Man means one/you in general; it is a subject only and is the normal way to speak about people in general.|**Man** is the impersonal pronoun meaning one, you or people. It can only be a **subject**, and it is the everyday way to generalise, much more common than the formal English one.¶• **Hur säger man det på svenska?** (How do you say that in Swedish?)¶• **Man gör så gott man kan.** (You do what you can.)¶• **I stan är man mer anonym.** (In the city you are more anonymous.)¶• **Man kan alltid lita på henne.** (You can always count on her.)¶Careful: **en man** is also a noun meaning man or husband. The pronoun is stressed weakly and is never capitalised.¶Related forms: the object is **en** (**Det kan göra en glad**, it can make you happy), and the reflexive possessive is **sin / sitt / sina**: **Man tror inte sina ögon.** (You can't believe your eyes.) Mistake: using man for a specific person or mixing it with du in the same sentence.
C1|pronouns|Reflexive possessive: sin, sitt, sina|466,496,500,552,583,588,642,675,696,743,3982|Use sin/sitt/sina when the owner is the subject; use hans/hennes/deras for someone else's.|The reflexive possessive **sin / sitt / sina** refers back to the **subject of the clause** (third person only). It agrees with the thing owned, not the owner.¶T:Owned noun¦Form¦Example//en-word¦sin¦Han tar hand om sin mamma.//ett-word¦sitt¦De väntar sitt andra barn.//plural¦sina¦Hon älskar sina barn.¶• **Han tar hand om sin sjuka mamma.** (He looks after his own sick mother.)¶• **Han tar hand om hans mamma.** means the mother of another man.¶• Use **hans, hennes, deras** when the owner is not the subject: **Jag träffade henne och hennes man.**¶• For I, you, we, the normal possessives stay: **min, din, vår**. Never use sin with jag or du.¶Tip for English speakers: English has one word for both cases, so this distinction has to be learned deliberately.
C1|pronouns|Emphatic and reflexive själv|245,957,1197,1424,1925,2183,2349,2741,3314|Själv adds emphasis (myself), and mig själv, sig själv reinforce a reflexive object.|**Själv** works in two ways.¶• Emphasis, agreeing with the subject (själv, självt, själva): **Jag har bakat kakan själv.** (I baked the cake myself.) **Vi har renoverat själva.** (We renovated ourselves.)¶• Reflexive object: the reflexive pronoun plus själv: **mig själv, dig själv, sig själv, oss själva**. **Han överträffade sig själv.** (He surpassed himself.) **Jag borde ta bättre hand om mig själv.** (I should take better care of myself.)¶Mind the difference between plain sig and sig själv:¶• **Han tvättar sig.** (He washes himself, normal.)¶• **Han tvättar sig själv.** (He washes himself, pointing out that he does it alone.)¶Själv also means alone in some phrases: **för mig själv** (on my own). **Håll det för dig själv.** (Keep it to yourself.) Tip: själv is not a pronoun on its own; it always needs a partner or sits after the subject.
C1|pronouns|Reciprocal varandra|235,491,557,577,585,598,612,685,711,716|Varandra means each other and takes a preposition like any object; it never changes.|**Varandra** (each other) is invariable and used as an object or after a preposition. It points back to a plural subject.¶• **Vi har känt varandra sedan skoltiden.** (We've known each other since school.)¶• **De tål inte varandra.** (They can't stand each other.)¶• **Vi står varandra väldigt nära.** (We are very close to each other.)¶• **Vi stötte ihop med varandra.** (We bumped into each other.)¶The preposition comes first and varandra follows: **till varandra, med varandra, för varandra**. Compare English each other, where the preposition can differ.¶The alternative **de/vi ... sig/oss emellan** is also used: **Det stannar mellan oss.** (That stays between us.) Mistake: using sig instead of varandra when you mean mutual action. De hälsar på sig can only mean each of them greets himself.
C1|pronouns|Relative den som, det som and the free relative|154,1150,1161,2791,2999,3117,125,3404|Den som means whoever or anyone who; det som and vad som mean what or that which.|Swedish builds headless relatives with **som**. It works like English whoever or what.¶• **Den som reser har något att berätta.** (Anyone who travels has stories to tell.)¶• **De som bott här länge trängs undan.** (Those who have lived here a long time are being pushed out.)¶• **Det som räknas är att du försöker.** (What counts is that you try.)¶• **Jag är nyfiken på vad som händer.** (I'm curious what is happening.)¶Remember **som** is the usual relative word and must be used instead of English who or which: **Det är inte det som är poängen.** (That is not the point.)¶• **Den/det/de** before som is the antecedent. **Den som köper billigt köper två gånger.** (Buy cheap, buy twice.)¶• **Vad som** + verb is used for indirect questions and what-clauses: **vad som händer**.¶• If som is the object, it can be dropped: **Det jag vill säga är...** (What I want to say is...).
C1|pronouns|Quantifiers: varje, var och en, båda, alla|601,736,1101,1104,1120,1534,1151,655,1062|Varje and var och en mean every/each, båda means both, and någon som helst means any at all.|These words express how many of a group you mean.¶• **Varje** (every, each) is always followed by a singular noun: **varje år**, **varje ord**. **Hyran justeras varje år.** (The rent is adjusted every year.) **På varje lägenhet kommer det hundra sökande.** (There are a hundred applicants for every apartment.)¶• **Var och en** (each one, everybody) stands alone: **Hos oss lagar var och en som den vill.** (At our place everyone cooks as they like.)¶• **Båda** (both): **Barnet bor hos båda föräldrarna.** (The child lives with both parents.)¶• **Alla** (all, everyone): **Skilsmässan var svår för alla.** (The divorce was hard on everyone.) **Här känner alla alla.** (Here everyone knows everyone.)¶• **Någon / något som helst** (any at all): **Jag har ingen aning alls.** or **Har du några problem som helst?** (Do you have any problems at all?)¶Tip: varje takes the noun singular, but alla takes the plural.
C1|adjectives|Comparison and irregular forms|424,425,767,1087,1128,1134,1140,1175,178|Add -are/-ast, use mer/mest for long adjectives, and learn the irregular good, bad, little, much.|Regular adjectives form the comparative with **-are** and the superlative with **-ast**: **snabb, snabbare, snabbast**; **stor** is irregular (**större, störst**). Long adjectives use **mer** and **mest**: **mer anonym**, **mest intressant**.¶• Regular: **Min bror är äldre än jag.** (My brother is older than me.) **Min syster är yngre.** (My sister is younger.)¶• Irregular (learn them): **bra, bättre, bäst**; **dålig, sämre, sämst**; **liten, mindre, minst**; **mycket, mer, mest**; **gammal, äldre, äldst**.¶• **Hemma kan jag koppla av bäst.** (At home I relax best.)¶• **Mindre är mer.** (Less is more.)¶• **Vi tillbringar mest tid i köket.** (We spend most time in the kitchen.)¶• **Än** = than: **Jag är äldre än du.**¶Mistake: using the English pattern more big. Say **större**.
C1|adjectives|Ju ... desto: the more, the more|1377,5515,6114,6115|Ju + comparative ... desto + comparative links two parallel changes.|To say that two things increase together, use **ju + comparative ... desto + comparative**, much like English the more ... the more. Both parts contain a comparative.¶• **Ju fler kockar, desto sämre soppa.** (Too many cooks spoil the broth.)¶• **Ju mer vi vet, desto mer inser vi hur mycket vi inte vet.** (The more we know, the more we realise how much we don't know.)¶• **Ju längre vi väntar, desto dyrare blir det.** (The longer we wait, the more expensive it gets.)¶The first clause is subordinate, so the verb follows the subject and the adverb: **Ju mer man tänker på det**. The second clause has verb second after desto: **desto krångligare blir det**.¶In conversation, ju ... ju is common as well: **Ju förr, desto bättre.** (The sooner, the better.) Do not use the before comparatives like in English.
C1|adjectives|Adjectives used as nouns|4174,4569,4852,5840,6005|Neuter det + adjective names an abstract idea; de + adjective means a group of people.|An adjective can stand alone as a noun in Swedish. The definite -a form is used.¶• **Det + adjective** names an abstract idea or quality: **Det goda tar tid.** (Good things take time.) **Förändring börjar i det lilla.** (Change starts small.)¶• **De + adjective** means a group of people: **de rika industriländerna**, **de gamla** (the old), **de unga** (the young), **de arbetslösa** (the unemployed).¶• **De gamla sederna hålls vid liv.** (The old customs are kept alive.)¶• For a single person you usually need a noun: **en gammal man**, not en gammal.¶Words like **de sjuka** are not offensive; the style is neutral. Some adjectives have become real nouns with their own plural: **en sjuk, sjuka** or **den sökande** (the applicant). Tip: English also says the rich and the poor, but Swedish uses this pattern much more widely.
C1|adjectives|Participles used as adjectives|3521,4540,5482,2173,1920,363,1936,3584,4492|Present participles end in -ande/-ende and describe qualities; past participles in -d/-t describe a state.|**Present participle** (**-ande / -ende**) is used as an adjective and describes an ongoing or characteristic quality. It does not change for gender or number.¶• **Förebyggande arbete måste få mer stöd.** (Preventive work needs more support.)¶• **De regerande mästarna är utslagna.** (The reigning champions are out.)¶• **Det är imponerande.** (That is impressive.)¶• **Den sökande gjorde ett utmärkt intryck.** (The applicant made an excellent impression.)¶**Past participle** describes a result and agrees with the noun (-d/-t, -da/-de):¶• **Affären är stängd.** (The shop is closed.)¶• **Jag känner mig inte uppskattad.** (I don't feel valued.)¶• **Mottagningen är stängd på grund av semester.**¶Tip: **-ande** is frequent in formal and written Swedish, and English -ing often corresponds to it (but not for a progressive verb: use håller på att).
C1|preps|Time prepositions: om, i, inom, sedan|54,456,607,1312,1668,3447,4056,4063,4211,491,1925|Om = in (future), i = for (duration), sedan = since/ago, inom = within.|Time prepositions mark when, how long and since when.¶• **Om** + time = in (the future): **Jag är där om tio minuter.** (I'll be there in ten minutes.) **Om en vecka.** (In a week.) **Om fem år** (in five years).¶• **I** + time = for (duration up to now): **Vi har varit tillsammans i fem år.** (We've been together for five years.) **Jag har jobbat här i tre år.**¶• **Sedan** + point in time = since: **Vi har känt varandra sedan skoltiden.** (We've known each other since school.)¶• **Sedan** after a time = ago: **för tre år sedan**.¶• **Inom** = within: **Vi ses inom kort.** (See you soon.)¶• **Till** = until, **fram till** = up to.¶Mistake: using for in the English way. Swedish does not use för for duration: say **i fem år**, not för fem år.
C1|preps|Compound prepositions: på grund av, i stället för|2130,2249,2646,3584,3116,3148,4955,2266,3508,6123|Multi-word prepositions give reasons and contrast in formal writing.|Many longer prepositions are fixed phrases. They connect a noun phrase (not a clause) to the sentence.¶• **På grund av** (because of, due to): **På grund av ett signalfel blir det en fördröjning.** (Because of a signal failure there is a delay.) **Mottagningen är stängd på grund av semester.**¶• **I stället för** (instead of): **Jag satsar på hållbarhet i stället för trender.** (I go for sustainability instead of trends.) With a verb: **i stället för att köpa**.¶• **Trots** (despite): **Trots alla ansträngningar lyckades det inte.**¶• **Enligt** (according to): **Jag tränar enligt ett schema.** **Tillfrisknandet går enligt plan.**¶• Also: **tack vare** (thanks to), **med hjälp av** (with the help of).¶Remember: before a full clause use the conjunction (**eftersom, trots att**), not the preposition.
C1|preps|Prepositions with adjectives: stolt över, rädd för|501,545,1674,1776,1821,2111,2152,2575,2754,3315|Adjective + preposition pairs must be learned as chunks; they rarely match English.|Many adjectives need a particular preposition, and it often differs from English.¶• **stolt över** (proud of): **Jag är stolt över dig.**¶• **förälskad i** (in love with): **Jag är helt förälskad i henne.**¶• **ansvarig för** (responsible for): **Jag är ansvarig för marknadsföringen.**¶• **nöjd med** (happy with): **Jag är nöjd med mitt jobb.**¶• **intresserad av** (interested in): **Jag är inte intresserad av sport.**¶• **beroende av** (dependent on): **Jag är beroende av klättring.**¶• **trött på** (tired of): **Jag är trött på att resa.**¶• **rädd om** (take care of) versus **rädd för** (afraid of): **Jag är rädd om min hälsa.**¶Tip: the preposition may be followed by att + infinitive: **trött på att resa**. C1|conj|Concession: även om, fastän, fast, ändå|2694,6121,6122,337,3565,168,738|Även om, fastän and fast open a concession; ändå and trots allt add 'still' in the main clause.|To say although, use a subordinate clause with **även om**, **fastän** or the more spoken **fast**.¶• **Även om målet är rätt är vägen dit fel.** (Even if the goal is right, the way there is wrong.)¶• **Fastän siffrorna ser bra ut är jag fortfarande försiktig.** (Although the numbers look good, I remain cautious.)¶• **Jag längtar redan ut igen, fast jag precis har kommit hem.** (I'm longing to go out again, even though I've just come home.)¶The adverbs **ändå** and **trots allt** express concession inside the main clause:¶• **Jag släpar mig till jobbet ändå.** (I drag myself to work anyway.)¶• **Blod är trots allt tjockare än vatten.** (Blood is thicker than water after all.)¶• **Som tur var gick det ändå.** (Luckily it worked out anyway.)¶Pitfall: **trots** is a preposition (trots regnet) and needs att before a clause: **trots att**. C1|conj|Paired conjunctions: både ... och, varken ... eller|4679,5221,5747,5990,6111,2599,1396,3987,6113|Både ... och, varken ... eller and inte bara ... utan även link two parts of equal weight.|These pairs link two equal elements.¶• **Både ... och** (both ... and): **Tekniken är både en välsignelse och en förbannelse.** (Technology is both a blessing and a curse.) **Globaliseringen har både vinnare och förlorare.**¶• **Varken ... eller** (neither ... nor): **Det gör varken från eller till.** (That makes no difference.) **Jag vet varken ut eller in.** (I'm at a loss.)¶• **Inte bara ... utan även / också** (not only ... but also): **Inte bara kostnaderna utan även arbetsinsatsen är enorm.** (Not only the cost but also the effort is huge.)¶• **Såväl ... som** is the formal alternative to både ... och.¶Rules: the two parts should have the same grammatical form, and **varken ... eller** already contains the negation, so don't add inte. After inte bara at the start, the verb is second: **Inte bara är det dyrt, utan...**
C1|conj|Purpose and reason: för att, eftersom, så att|980,2269,2271,2638,2717,2758,3342,5427,2086,4529|För att + infinitive gives a purpose, eftersom a reason, and så att a result or aim.|Three small connectors express why.¶• **För att + infinitive** (in order to): **Jag tränar för att rensa huvudet.** (I exercise to clear my head.) **Man behöver visum för att resa in.** (You need a visa to enter.) C1|conj|Time clauses: när, medan, innan, tills|113,208,248,294,1006,1378,4105,4108|När covers when/whenever, medan means while, innan before and tills until; då is mostly a past-time adverb.|Swedish **när** is the all-purpose when, for past, present and future. C1|neg|Ingen, inget, aldrig: negative pronouns and adverbs|57,58,87,142,156,331,341,109,269,2400|Ingen, ingenting, inget and aldrig carry the negation themselves, so inte is not added.|Negative words replace inte and the matching positive word, so Swedish avoids double negatives.¶• **ingen** (no, nobody, en-word) / **inget** (no, nothing, ett-word) / **inga** (plural): **Om jag ska vara ärlig har jag ingen lust.** (To be honest I have no desire.) **Uppriktigt sagt hade jag ingen aning.**¶• **ingenting** / **ingenstans**: **Jag fattar ingenting.** (I don't understand a thing.) **Det gör ingenting.** (That doesn't matter.)¶• **aldrig**: **Han ger aldrig upp förrän slutsignalen går.** (He never gives up until the final whistle.)¶Compare: **Jag har inte någon lust** is also possible but sounds more formal than ingen lust. C1|neg|Understatement: inte illa, inte direkt, inte alls|358,1395,322,67,268,64,162,464|Swedes soften and understate with inte + adjective or adverb: inte illa, inte direkt, inte så.|Swedish often says less than it means, using a negative to soften.¶• **Det var inte illa!** (That was quite something!, i.e. good)¶• **Det är inte direkt idealiskt.** (That's not exactly ideal.)¶• **Inte så bra, om jag ska vara ärlig.** (Not so good, to be honest.)¶• **Inte så farligt.** (It's no big deal.)¶• **Det var inte alls min avsikt.** (That was not at all my intention.)¶• **Vi ses inte så ofta.** (We don't see each other that often.)¶Watch out: **inte så** can mean not very (**inte så bra**) or not that way (**Det var inte så jag menade**). **Inte alls** is firm, but **inte direkt** and **inte helt** tone things down. C1|neg|Förrän, inte bara, inte minst|1375,2176,2400,4376,2372,4526,6054,6113,6146,6211|Inte ... förrän means not until; inte bara and inte minst give nuance beyond plain negation.|• **Inte ... förrän** (not until, only when): **Det är inte över förrän domaren blåser av.** (It's not over until the referee blows.) **Jag hinner inte med det förrän i slutet av nästa vecka.** (I won't get to it until the end of next week.) The negative stays in the main clause and **förrän** introduces the time. **Det blir ingen efterrätt förrän du har ätit upp grönsakerna.**¶• **Inte bara** (not just): **Det är inte bara ett spel, det är en passion.**¶• **Inte minst** (not least): **Sist men inte minst vill jag tacka alla inblandade.** (Last but not least I thank everyone involved.)¶• **Inte ens** (not even): **inte ens med maten**.¶Mistake: using först or bara in place of förrän for until. Förrän always needs a negative or a negative-like word in the main clause.
C1|neg|Tag questions: eller hur, va, väl|202,277,116,312|Eller hur, va and väl ask for confirmation or soften a statement into a question.|Swedish confirms with short tags.¶• **Eller hur?** (right? isn't it?): **Vi har inte träffats förut, eller hur?** (We haven't met before, have we?)¶• **Va?** (informal, right?): **Du skämtar, va?** (You're joking, right?)¶• **Väl** inside the sentence turns it into a hopeful question: **Jag stör väl inte?** (I'm not disturbing you, am I?)¶• **Inte sant?** is a bit more formal.¶There is no change of tag for tense or person, unlike English isn't it, haven't you; **eller hur** works for everything. Intonation rises. In writing, use it only in dialogue or informal texts. The tag **väl** stays in the middle of the clause: **Det var väl självklart.** (It was surely obvious.)
C1|mood|Passive with modal verbs: måste beslutas|1905,3296,3446,3450,3587,1090,5083,216|Modal verb + s-passive infinitive states rules, needs and possibilities without naming an actor.|The s-passive works well after modal verbs and gives a neutral, impersonal tone.¶• **Det måste beslutas på högsta nivå.** (That has to be decided at the highest level.)¶• **Receptet måste hämtas ut inom 28 dagar.** (The prescription must be collected within 28 days.)¶• **Såret måste sys.** (The wound needs stitches.)¶• **Det där kan slängas.** (That can be thrown away.)¶• **Orden måste följas av handling.** (Words must be followed by deeds.)¶The infinitive is formed by adding **-s**: **beslutas, hämtas, sys, slängas**. The same -s ending can also mean reciprocal action (**vi ses**), so check context.

C1|mood|Låt oss and låt mig: let us and let me|152,261,324,1738,1765,3892,3949,4000,6073,6180|Låt oss invites joint action; låt mig asks permission or states an intention.|**Låt** is the imperative of **låta** (let), followed by a pronoun and an infinitive without att.¶• **Låt oss** + infinitive (let us): **Låt oss snabbt sammanfatta.** (Let's quickly summarise.) **Låt oss blicka framåt.** (Let's look ahead.) **Låt oss diskutera det sakligt.**¶• **Låt mig** + infinitive (let me): **Låt mig prata klart!** (Let me finish!) **Låt mig förtydliga det.** (Let me clarify that.) **Låt mig sova på saken.** (Let me sleep on it.)¶Both are common in speeches, meetings and polite discussion. They also appear in the pattern **Låt mig påminna om att...** to introduce a point.¶Informal alternative to låt oss: **Vi tar och...** or **Ska vi...?** Mistake: Låt oss att gå. No att after låt oss/mig.
C1|numbers|Fractions, halv and percentages|1086,1297,1417,2166,2868,2890|Halv agrees with its noun (en halv, ett halvt, halva); prosent follows the number.|**Halv** (half) is an adjective and agrees with its noun.¶• **en halv** timme, **ett halvt** kilo, **halva** jobbet (plural/definite).¶• **Ett halvt kilo köttfärs, tack.** (Half a kilo of mince, please.)¶• **Vi har väntat i en halvtimme.** (We've waited half an hour.)¶• **Ordning och reda är halva jobbet.** (Tidiness is half the battle.)¶• **Jag springer mitt första halvmaraton.** (My first half marathon.)¶Percentages: the number is followed by **procent** with no change and no percent sign spelled out: **Det är 20 procent rabatt.**¶• Other fractions: **hälften** (the half), **en tredjedel**, **en fjärdedel**, **tre fjärdedelar**.¶• **Hälften av** + definite noun: **hälften av eleverna**.¶Tip: in time, **halv** means half an hour before the next hour: **halv tre** is 2.30.
C1|numbers|Ages, decades, dates and large numbers|17,412,607,970,1110,1827,2254,3171,5115,5367|Ages use år gammal, decades take -talet, dates use ordinals, and miljon is a noun with plural -er.|• **Age**: **Jag är trettio år gammal.** (I'm thirty.) **Min dotter är fem år gammal.** For birthdays: **När fyller du år?**¶• **Duration**: **i sextio år**, **efter fyrtio år**, **på trettio år** (over thirty years).¶• **Decades**: add **-talet**: **femtiotalet**, **nittiotalet**. **Huset är från femtiotalet.** (The house dates from the fifties.)¶• **Dates**: ordinals with **den**: **den första oktober**, **den femte maj**. **Jag börjar den första oktober.** The year is read in full: **tjugohundratjugoåtta** or **tvåtusen tjugoåtta**; **till 2028**.¶• **Large numbers**: **en miljon**, **två miljoner**, and a noun after them follows without of: **66 miljoner år sedan**. **Miljoner är på flykt.** (Millions are fleeing.)¶Tip: use a space as the thousands separator (1 000 000) and a comma for decimals.
C1|particles|Ju: shared knowledge and surprise|354,384,395,1599,2057,3759,3890,3983|Ju marks something as obvious or already known and adds reproach, surprise or reassurance.|The particle **ju** sits in the middle of the clause (after the verb in main clauses). It does not translate directly; it signals that the speaker treats the information as **known or obvious**.¶• **Det är ju strunt!** (That's nonsense, as you can see!)¶• **Man tappar ju andan.** (Well, it takes your breath away.)¶• **Domaren är ju blind!** (But the referee is blind!)¶• **Dig känner man ju knappt igen!** (You're hardly recognisable!)¶• **Nä men, det var ju toppen!** (Well, that's just great!, ironic)¶Used with a positive tone, ju is friendly reassurance: **Du vet ju hur det är.** (You know how it is.)¶Position: in subordinate clauses it goes before the verb (**eftersom det ju är sant**). Do not confuse it with **ju ... desto**. Tip: stressed ju can add irritation.
C1|particles|Nog: probably versus enough|235,323,3152,3960,6265,1192,1751,3718,3984,6242|Nog as a particle means probably or I suppose; after an adjective or as a noun phrase it means enough.|**Nog** has two uses that are easy to mix up.¶**1. C1|particles|Väl: assumption and tentative checking|116,312,6083,4615|Väl adds a tone of assuming agreement (surely, I suppose), and it also means well.|As a particle, **väl** says that the speaker expects agreement but wants to check. It is close to surely or I suppose.¶• **Jag stör väl inte?** (I'm not disturbing you, am I?)¶• **Det var väl självklart.** (It was surely obvious, the least I could do.)¶• **Man kan mycket väl hävda att det är vettigt.** (One can very well argue that it makes sense.)¶Compare the adverb **väl** meaning well:¶• **Podden är väl researchad.** (The podcast is well researched.)¶The particle usually stands after the finite verb and the subject. It is often found in questions with a negative: **Du kommer väl inte?** The difference to **ju**: ju states what both already know, väl asks whether it is so. Also related: **visst** and **nog**.

C1|particles|Alltså, förresten, ändå: discourse markers|120,326,2354,168,3565,738|Alltså, förresten and ändå steer a conversation: a conclusion, a change of topic or an unexpected outcome.|These small words organise speech.¶• **Alltså** (so, in other words, I mean): **Alltså: Vi måste skjuta upp alltihop.** (In other words: we have to postpone everything.) C1|punct|Commas: before men and between clauses|159,190,286,317,320,537,653,997,1131,1778|Put a comma before men; commas in Swedish are far less strict than in German and mark pauses and structure.|Swedish comma rules are lighter than in German. The core rules:¶• Before **men** (but): **Jag är ganska stressad, men annars bra.** (I'm pretty stressed, but otherwise fine.) **Det är inte optimalt, men det fungerar.**¶• In lists, between items except before the final **och**: **äpplen, päron och bananer**.¶• After a fronted clause, to show where the main clause starts: **Om jag ska vara ärlig, har jag ingen lust.**¶• Around inserted commentary: **Det här är pinsamt, men jag har glömt ditt namn.**¶• Before **och** only if it joins two long main clauses and could confuse the reader.¶• **Subordinate clauses** (att, som, eftersom): a comma is optional and often left out in short sentences, though it helps clarity.¶Do not put a comma before att in an ordinary reported statement: **Jag tror att det går bra.**
C1|punct|Compound words: one word, not two|939,1019,1118,2131,2294,2732,2768,5222,5301,5320|Write compounds as one word; split spelling changes meaning or is simply wrong.|Swedish compounds are written as **one word**, unlike many English compounds. The last part decides the gender and the plural.¶• **världsrekord** (world record), **världsmästare**, **världsarv** (heritage), **världsekonomin**¶• **lägenhetsvisning** (apartment viewing), **byggarbetsplats** (building site), **årsstämma** (annual meeting)¶• **Hon har satt världsrekord.** (She set the world record.)¶• **Företaget är världsledande inom sin nisch.** (The company is the world leader in its niche.)¶Often a linking letter **-s-** (or **-e-**, **-a-**) is inserted: **årsstämma**, **lägenhetsvisning**. It has to be learned by ear; the s does not belong to the first word's genitive.¶Splitting a compound is a typical Swedish error (called särskrivning) and can change the meaning: **en stor stad** or **en storstad**? Rule of thumb: if it is one idea, write it together. Long compounds are normal: **hälsoundersökning**. Hyphens appear with letters or numbers: **UNESCO-världsarv**, **3-åring**.

C1|style|Hedging and tact: med all respekt, om jag får fråga|315,316,318,319,190,317,159,307,308,253|Fixed polite frames let you disagree, ask or be frank without causing offence.|Frames that cushion what you say:¶• **Med all respekt, ...** (with all due respect): **Med all respekt, jag ser annorlunda på det.** **Med all respekt, så stämmer det inte riktigt.**¶• **Om jag får fråga: ...** (if I may ask): **Om jag får fråga: Vad jobbar du med?**¶• **Jag vill inte vara ... men ...**: **Jag vill inte vara indiskret, men hur gammal är du?** (I don't want to be indiscreet, but how old are you?)¶• **Ta inte illa upp, men ...** (don't take offence): **Ta inte illa upp om jag går tidigare.**¶• **Ursäkta att jag stör.** (Sorry for the interruption.)¶• **Hur ska jag säga?** (How shall I put it?)¶The pattern is: warn, then say the thing.
